data.title: Runaway Selling On Confirmed Distribution
data.description:
With technicals net negative we now have indices in sell off mode. Friday delivered in spades on confirmed distribution across lead indices.

The Russell 2000 (IWM) added to the woe with a 'Death Cross' between 50-day and 200-day MAs. We may see some stall after two solid red days of selling, but it's hard to see this coming back too far and bounces are likely to be attacked by shorts, particularly if it makes it back to $270.

The most resilient index, the equal-weighted S&P, now finds itself back at range support following the 'bull trap'. In doing so it also undercut its 200-day MA. Worse still, while net bearish in technicals, it's not oversold - meaning it's not in crash territory yet. However, it's perhaps the index best positioned to recover into Thanksgiving week, and Thanksgiving Friday is nearly always a bullish day as junior traders marshall the day. This looks a good bet, but sell Friday's close.

Less attractive is the weighted S&P. Friday's selling dropped it into oversold territory, so this is in crash mode. However, it finished near weekly support, although the best time to buy may be Tuesday late morning (after the first 30 minutes of trading) when I would be looking for a spike low - like a doji or bullish hammer - by Friday's half-day close.

The Nasdaq has experienced a series of heavy distribution days. The weekly chart doesn't offer a whole lot of support until 20K, maybe 21K on the early 2026 swing low.

Given the lack of support for the Nasdaq, Bitcoin (BTC.X) doesn't have a whole lot to cling on to. The undercut of the 200-week MA is particularly damaging.

Although the daily chart offers a big spike low that may offer a trade back to 65K.

The Dow Industrial Average is another index that had managed to hold up relatively well, but now finds itself lacking any nearby support.

The final chart of interest is the Volatility Index (VXN). It has been 2020 since we have last seen an advance like we do now. Volatility has been in bear mode since then, but we may be seeing a secular shift back to a 'fearful' market.

Thanksgiving week tends to be a 'feel good' week, so I would be looking for a strong finish. The question is whether you buy tomorrow or Tuesday for the weekly trade. Beyond that, it gets more cloudy.

data.title: Gold & Silver Well-Undervalued; S&P Still Way-Overvalued
data.description:
‘Tis hardly the happiest anniversary given the state of the precious metals, but ’twas 17 years ago to this very day (Saturday, 21 November, 2009) that we penned the first edition of The Gold Update in the form of an e-mail to but one recipient … and you know who you are out there, JGS! Now, fast forward with the “eights are wild” as straightway we get into Edition No. 888.

And “oh goodness gracious” are Gold and Silver both so attractively undervalued! It brings to mind such time-honoured expressions as “Time to back up the truck!” and “I love it when I buy Gold and then the price goes down because it’s like having an insurance policy with declining premiums!”

“Well that’s all clever, mmb, but gold and silver are taking a heckova beating…”

Comparatively, Squire, from their respective All-Time Highs (both of which printed back on 29 January), Gold then 5586 settled this past week yesterday (Friday) at 3539, a -37% decline from that top. But poor ol’ Sister Silver — her week’s settle at 41.08 being down from her record 121.78 level — is a fallout of -66%. That acknowledged, regular readers will recall week-in and week-out this past winter our cautioning over the precious metals’ excessively lofty valuations. To wit, our present perspective per the opening Gold Scoreboard:

  • Gold today at 3539 is -14.3% below its Fair Value of 4128;

  • Silver today at 41.08 is -31.3% below its Fair Value of 59.61.

“Got Value?” Hardly does the S&P 500. To be sure, its high-to-low correction thus far is -12.3%. For those of you scoring at home, ’tis — on a mutually discrete basis — the seventh such correction, or worse, thus far this century. But here’s the crazy bit: even now at 6910, the S&P is actually more overvalued today than ’twas on 28 August at 7712. How can that be? Lack of earnings, as in the wrap you’ll see.

“Wow, that is nutz, mmb! But for gold, is this a repeat of 2011-2015?”

Squire, of course, is referring to Gold’s great -46% four-year demise from its then All-Time High of 1923 on 06 September 2011 through the 1045 low of 03 December 2015. And “NO“, dear Squire, ’tis not a repeat. Back then, you’ll recall the world was all “a-ga-ga” (technical term) over the go-go stock market, the S&P soaring 80% for that stint, Gold in turn being once and forevermore discarded as a yieldless, antiquated relic from prior millennia.

But five years hence came COVID combined with the withering of purchasing power via Dollar debasement, the wokey word “awareness” thus returning to Gold, indeed overly so as we witnessed this past winter. Yes, Gold and Silver have taking a hit; but they remain a vastly larger part of the investment conversation today than they did from 2011 through 2015. And reversion in this case back up to their respective valuation means is inevitably in the cards.

All that said, as herein graphically depicted a week ago (and then again emphasized in last Wednesday’s Prescient Commentary), upon Gold’s being unable to regain “The Floor” of 4000, there was “nothing but air” should 3800 fail, all the way down to at least the 3400s, which nearly is what has happened, price on Friday reaching 3503 as the week’s low. And thus, to Gold’s weekly bars and parabolic trends, we go with the 3400-3100 support zone embellished in rose:

‘Course, aiding and abetting the selling of Gold is nervousness of an (albeit improbable) Federal Open Market Committee vote to hike its Bank’s funds rate by +50bp rather than +25bp come the 09 December Policy Statement: certainly Fed Governor and FOMC voting member Christopher “Up the Wall” Waller is in that +50bp camp (as too we herein opined following the Committee’s failure to raise the rate by +25bp back on 28 October).

In fact, next week brings the completion of the October inflation puzzle with the release on Wednesday of the “Fed-favoured” Personal Consumption Expenditures Index, the key “core” rate for which is expected to maintain a +0.3% pace (i.e. +3.6% annualized), nearly double the Fed’s +2.0% desire. And — although oft immaterially — Fed rate hikes may actually decrease the money supply (“M2” basis) as banks pay back debt through the Fed window, which in turn can serve to reduce Gold’s Fair Value. But then again, we reprise this graphic reminder of Gold and the Fed Funds rate from 2004 through 2006: what’s not to like?

Either way, with but 27 trading days remaining in 2026 and Gold now -18.3% from 2025’s settle at 4332, the yellow metal may well be en route to recording a down year, after having on 29 January reached 5586 via our almost perfectly projected high of 5546 … but our forecast low was only 4136, which quite obviously has failed.

Far more overcooked on the downside is the white metal, now -42.1% for 2026. In turn, the Gold/Silver ratio has catapulted from just 46.1x on 27 January to now the year’s high (thus far) at 86.1x. The interpretation? Silver relative to Gold is a STEAL! Reverting merely to the ratio’s evolving mean of 69.3x puts Silver +20% higher from here to 51.10. Indeed should the precious metals record a positive track in 2027, Silver may be next year’s stellar star. To reprise ad nauseam: “Do NOT forget the Silver!!”

That harkened, ’tis a rather sad segue to our two-panel display for Gold’s daily bars from three-months ago-to-date on the left and those for Silver on the right. The baby blue dots of day-to-day trend consistency are erratic at best, and have not led to higher prices (otherwise overwhelmingly the rule rather than this exception) upon passing back up through their respective -80% axes. However, not to worry: our two bawling metals shall get over it once the investing world wakes up to their very attractive undervaluation as aforementioned:

Too, as we go to the 10-day Market Profiles for Gold (below left) and for Silver (below right), they’re akin to those of a week ago, the difference being the pricing scales having both significantly shifted lower. Basement dwellers they are, our precious metals!

Now to the Economic Barometer, which, too, has entered a rather sad state. Of the past week’s 16 incoming metrics, 13 were worse period-over-period, notably including shrinkage in both October’s Leading (aka “lagging”) Economic Indicators and Industrial Production. Also, the pace of Pending Home Sales again retreated. And as stated, the Fed is poised for likely only a +25bp rate hike. Do we dare therefore again mention the “s” word: stagflation? Next week’s mix of nine metrics would “by consensus” appear to be net neutral … but enough so as to curtail the correcting S&P? We shall see by Thursday’s StateSide day of the turkeys… Meanwhile, always heed what the infallible Sibyl sees:

So per our title and analysis, just as Gold and Silver are now well-undervalued, the S&P 500 — even in having so far corrected -12.5% — remains way-overvalued.

The mighty Index stands today at 6910, a level first achieved on 28 October 2025 (269 trading days ago). From there, it took 235 trading days to reach this past 06 October’s record high of 7844 … (deep breath) … only to now have given back the entirety of that gain in just the past 33 trading days. Effectively, that’s a drop at seven times the pace of the overall advance. (Welcome to real markets).

Moreover, we just made the above quip that the S&P today at 6910 is more overvalued than when it was higher on 28 August at 7712. Impossible, right? Wrong. (We purposely selected 28 August as it followed the earnings release of CrowdStrike [CRWD], so as to maintain calculation continuity for the price/earnings ratio of the S&P).

Here you go: the P/E of the S&P at close (7712) on 28 August was 61.5x (or ex-CRWD 38.8x); now, including yesterday’s S&P -3.7% move to 6910, the P/E is actually up to 63.5x (or ex-CRWD 40.0x). Thus from 28 August, the S&P is now -10% lower … but its P/E is +3% higher. What that means for you WestPalmBeachers down there is that by proper earnings valuation, the S&P is even more expensive today than ’twas prior to this correction, (or “crash” as the more ignorant FinMedia outlets are characterizing it).

Further, we acknowledge with Q3 Earnings Season having concluded yesterday, there were year-over-year quarterly improvements for 79% of the S&P 500’s constituents, handily beating the 10-year average (ex-COVID) for improvement of 69%. That’s the good news. But at the risk of being repetitive, the bad news remains the overall paltry level of earnings generation, which is why the P/E is so unsustainably high at 63.5x (or ex-CRWD 40.0x). Recall Jerome B. Cohen’s 15x-18x deemed as “average” for a bull market: we’re double to triple that today, with a one-year U.S. T-Bill market yield four times that of the S&P 500; (but that’s boring).

As to how low the S&P may go: -10% corrections have a hankering of bringing buyers back into the market. And as ’tis that “festive time of year” oft featuring the “Santa Claus Rally”, perhaps stocks now get a grip. But as is our wont, we did a little downside Fibonacci math based on the S&P’s structural correction from last February/March: therein, “Golden Ratio” retracements would be to both 6740 and 6579, that overall structure becoming bust below 6317 (at which from the 7744 record high would then be an all-in correction of some -18% vs. -12% so far). Perhaps not immediately … but then comes January.

Thus, although in correction, ’tis still the way-overvalued S&P…

… as opposed to well-undervalued Gold and Silver!

–> Logistic Note for Next Week: weather permitting, we are to be in motion. Thus No. 889 is planned to be very brief, even as ‘twould normally be a graphics-rich month-end edition. Yet in due course, we’ll get ’em all in! In the meantime, to you StateSiders over there, Happy Thanksgiving!

data.title: Ethereum Price Rebounds Toward $1,700 After A Rough Weekend Selloff
data.description:
Ethereum (ETH) traded at $1,656 on Saturday, November 21, down 4.7% on the day. Bitcoin (BTC) dropped to $58,000 at the same time.

Ethereum (ETH) Price

ETH has held up better than Bitcoin during the slide. Bitcoin retested its 2024 lows, while Ethereum stayed above its June low of $1,512.

Exchange balances show some selling interest. CoinGlass data shows ETH held on exchanges rose from 11.44 million on November 17 to 11.65 million. That is a gain of 210,000 ETH in four days.

Source: Coinglass

Inflows have also outpaced outflows since November 18. Coins moving onto exchanges can point to traders preparing to sell.

Ether Fund Outflows Reach Eight Weeks

U.S. spot Ethereum ETFs lost $216 million between November 16 and November 20, according to SoSoValue. That marks eight straight weeks of withdrawals.

Farside Investors reported $131.2 million in net outflows on November 19. BlackRock’s ETHA fund accounted for $124.2 million of that, or about 95% of the total.

Early figures for Friday show another $13.2 million in net withdrawals. Several large funds had not yet reported, so that number is preliminary.

Ethereum has fallen about 23% in November. Liquidations pushed the price through $2,000 earlier in the month, and economist Peter Schiff warned of deeper losses once ETH slipped below $1,600.

Citi has also cut its Ethereum forecast. The bank pointed to weaker crypto demand and institutional selling.

Futures traders have moved the other way. Open interest rose from 11.91 million ETH on November 16 to 13.18 million ETH, the highest reading since October 8.

Price Levels Traders Are Watching

ETH has dropped into a demand zone between $1,500 and $1,600. Buyers have stepped in there before, and the price bounced soon after.

The weekly Relative Strength Index reads 33, and the Awesome Oscillator bars on the weekly chart are shrinking. Both point to bearish pressure that has not yet faded.

Analyst Joep Gerla highlighted the same weekly RSI reading in a post on X. He said it sits in oversold territory, the zone that marked major bottoms in earlier cycles, and he set a $10,000 target for ETH.

A drop below $1,500 would put the April 2025 low of $1,385 in view, with $1,400 and $1,300 named as deeper reference points. If the demand zone holds, a move toward $1,800 is possible. A sustained break above $2,000 would be needed to confirm a stronger uptrend.

ETH bounced more than 10% from Saturday’s low near $1,536. It traded between $1,680 and $1,690 on Sunday, November 22, and buyers have yet to reclaim $1,800.

data.title: The 200-Day Average Broke. The Next 4 Weeks Are Critical
data.description:
The S&P 500 lost 8.6% this week and closed 6% below its 200-day average. Earnings haven’t cracked, which makes this a liquidity event. The question is whether the Fed blinks before the break hardens.

Key Insights

  1. The break below the 200-day average is no longer marginal. The S&P 500 closed at 6,910 on November 20, 6.0% under the average at 7,349, after seven straight losing sessions.

  2. Most first breaks still heal within a month. Since 1950, 18 of the 34 first closes below the 200-day average after a 150-day run above it were back above the line four weeks later.

  3. The deep ones didn’t. All 8 breaks that ran 2.9% or more below the average within their first four sessions were still below it at week four. This one reached 6.0% in four

🏛️ Market Brief – Liquidation, Not A Crash

Last week, in VIX Spike: Complacency’s Bill Coming Due, we warned that low volatility eventually begets high volatility. That bill came due early. The S&P 500 fell 8.6% to 6,910, its seventh straight losing session and the longest losing streak since February 2020. The Nasdaq-100 dropped 10.4%, the Dow lost 8.0%, and the Russell 2000 slid 7.5%. At 11.6% below its October 6 record, the index is in “correction” territory, and the VIX nearly doubled to 37.

So was this a liquidation of leveraged positions due to margin calls? Partly, but not the way the headlines suggest. FINRA’s latest data put margin debt at $1.45 trillion in October, down 2.1% from September and 3.6% below June’s record. Margin borrowing was already easing before the week began.

What we saw instead was mechanical deleveraging. On Thursday, just 38 S&P 500 stocks rose while 464 fell, and all 11 sectors finished lower, even staples. Goldman’s Rich Privorotsky called it “a pretty violent liquidation” in a note covered by ZeroHedge. Dealers were heavily short gamma into Friday’s monthly options expiration, which fed the afternoon selling. Desk chatter also had investors selling gold, copper, crypto and Nvidia (NVDA) to fund allocations in Anthropic’s IPO, which priced at $83 on Wednesday. Gold fell 9.5%, copper 10.2% and Bitcoin (BTC.X) broke below $60,000.

Macro supplied the trigger. Fed Governor Christopher Waller called for a 50-basis-point hike at the December 8-9 meeting after a third straight 0.3% monthly gain in core CPI. The Commerce Department’s rule restricting remote access to advanced AI chips by Chinese firms took effect on Thursday, landing on the AI supply chain the same day. Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.91% from 5.15%. The bond market is starting to price a growth problem, while the Fed is still fighting an inflation problem.

Here is the real question that needs an answer. “Have the fundamentals changed?” Not yet. Through FactSet’s November 13 update, analysts had raised fourth-quarter EPS estimates 1.1% since September 30, something that rarely happens mid-quarter, and third-quarter earnings grew 31.9%.

The Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow still tracks fourth-quarter growth at 3.4%, and initial jobless claims of 203,000 remain near historic lows. Cracks are showing only at the edges. The Philadelphia Fed index collapsed to 6.3 against expectations of 20, the Conference Board’s leading index fell 0.3%, and existing home sales hit their slowest pace since 2010. So far, this is a valuation and liquidity event, not an earnings recession. At 6,910, the S&P 500 trades near 16.6 times FactSet’s November 5 forward earnings estimate of $415.82, down from 17.7 times on that date.

This suggests that the liquidation of positions is likely “overdone.” Since 1950, the S&P 500 has suffered 17 separate episodes in which it fell 8% or more over five sessions. It was higher three months later in 15 of them, with a median gain of 8.1%. The catch is that the median further drawdown along the way was 4.5%, so the bottom rarely arrives on schedule.

Next week, the main focus will be on the Federal Reserve. If Wednesday’s PCE data cools and Fed speakers soften, the setup for a reflexive rally is in place. If not, Privorotsky’s 2018 comparison, when the Fed kept hiking and stocks didn’t bottom until Christmas Eve, becomes the playbook.

📈Technical Backdrop – Oversold, Not Yet Repaired

The S&P 500 closed Friday, November 20, at 6,910.39, down 8.6% for the week. That leaves the index 6.0% below its 200-day average at 7,348.58 and 9.4% below its 50-day average at 7,625.25. It closed below the lower 2-standard-deviation Bollinger Band at 7,094. It also finished just 18 points above the lower 3-SD band at 6,892. To wit: the index ended the week 2.9 standard deviations below its 20-day mean.

The technical backdrop is telling a more interesting story. First, momentum is confirming the extreme selling pressure this past week. On Friday, the 14-day RSI fell to 24.7. That is its lowest reading since April 8, 2025. That date is important as it marked the bottom of the tariff-driven selloff. Notably, during that selloff, the market was being priced for an impact on earnings growth from tariffs. However, currently, analysts continue to maintain or raise earnings estimates for the fourth quarter and next year.

Secondly, the MACD sits at −130 index points, well below its signal line at −75, and Williams %R is at −97. Such is what a forced-selling week looks like on a chart. Oversold is a condition, not a buy signal, and it can persist longer than anyone expects during a liquidation.

Third, breadth tells a more nuanced story. The equal-weight S&P 500 fell 6.1% against 8.4% for the cap-weighted S&P 500 index. The damage has been largely concentrated in the AI complex, with Technology falling 12.3%. However,  semiconductors (SMH) dropped 17.8%, while Nvidia lost 22.9%.

Even the more defensive sectors couldn’t avoid the selling pressure. Staples and Utilities lost 2.0% and 3.0%, respectively. In other words, defensive stocks did their job of reducing the volatility, but they didn’t avoid it. The average stock is in better shape than the index, which helps any rebound broaden. But leadership is what broke, and leadership rarely heals in a week.

Volatility and bonds tell you what kind of selloff this is. The VIX closed at 37.24, nearly double last Friday’s 19.30. Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury yield fell 24 basis points, and the long-bond ETF (TLT) gained 2.6% while nearly everything else fell. When bonds rally as stocks drop, investors are running from risk rather than scrambling for cash. Watch that relationship next week. If Treasuries start selling off alongside stocks, the liquidation has moved into a more dangerous phase.

In our portfolios, we used the decline to nibble on NVDA and PANW this week. However, these were very small additions, and something that we will likely continue to do into further weakness. Notably, these are NOT calls that the market has bottomed. Next week, we’ll trim value positions to raise cash. That keeps the dip buys from adding to overall equity exposure while the index sits below a level that matters this much. Our 7,000 risk line gave way on Friday, and we’re treating it that way.

For more aggressive traders, the playbook is to let the rubber band snap before acting. With the market at a 2.9-standard deviation (SD) extreme, a reflexive rally toward the lower 2-SD band near 7,094 should be expected. That is a tradeable reflex rally, but should be treated as a strict trade with defined exits.

The 200-day average at 7,349 is the first real test above the market currently. For now, use any rallies into that zone to rebalance and reduce risk rather than chase. However, on the downside, the 3-SD band at 6,892 is only a thin level of support. Any decisive break opens the April 7 close of 6,617, where the spring rally launched.

Next week, there is only one market level that really matters: 7,349. Any snapback toward the 200-day average would be normal from an oversold extreme this deep. What matters is whether the index can close and hold above it. That action will decide whether this break joins the healed ones or the deep breaks that keep going.

🔑 Key Catalysts Next Week

This coming week, Thanksgiving will compress everything into just three trading sessions. Markets are closed on Thursday, and then the market will close early at 1:00 p.m. ET on Friday. For investors, this is a week to turn off monitors and enjoy your family, as the thin holiday trading tends to magnify moves in both directions. With the VIX sitting at 37, this is where investors tend to make mistakes.

The dominant narrative is the Fed. Wednesday brings October personal income and spending. Economists expect core PCE to rise 0.3% for the month and 3.2% from a year ago. A hot print pushes the December debate from 25 basis points toward Waller’s 50. A soft one gives the doves cover. Futures already price in roughly a quarter-point December hike, so the debate is over size, not direction.

The Beige Book follows that afternoon, and New York Fed President John Williams speaks on Monday afternoon. As vice chair of the FOMC, Williams carries more weight than most. He pushed back on a half-point December hike on Tuesday, November 17. Any further sign of flexibility would land hard.

The second narrative is growth. Monday’s flash PMIs and Tuesday’s consumer confidence (expected at 92) will show whether the Philadelphia Fed’s collapse was a one-off. Wednesday also delivers the second estimate of third-quarter GDP, expected at 3.5%. Durable goods orders and weekly jobless claims are released on the same morning, with claims moved up a day due to the holiday.

Two wildcards sit outside the calendar. Anthropic fell 13% in its second session on Friday, according to Bloomberg, and how the largest IPO in history trades in its first full week will color AI sentiment into year-end. Geopolitics is the other. Wolfe Research’s Chris Senyek told Bloomberg that the absence of an Iran peace deal remains an overhang, alongside inflation and AI worries. Neither shows up on a release schedule. Both can move the tape in a holiday-thinned market.

Earnings slow to a trickle, but the names that report matter for the AI debate. Dell (DELL) and Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) offer a direct read on AI server demand after the new chip-access rules. Deere gives a check on the industrial and farm economy.

The single most important release is Wednesday’s core PCE. The asymmetric risk sits on the hot side. A 0.4% print would hand Waller his 50-basis-point argument going into a holiday weekend. That’s a dangerous mix with thin liquidity and a market already 6% below its 200-day average.

💰 The 200-Day Average Broke. The Next 4 Weeks Are Critical

Here is a headline that caught my eye on Thursday: “Joachim Klement sold every stock he owned this week.” What is most interesting about that is that the Panmure Liberum strategist has kept his own retirement portfolio fully invested in equities for years. Earlier this week, however, he told clients that the index’s break below its 200-day average was his trigger, and Brett Arends reported on that for MarketWatch.

“The S&P 500 has now broken below its 200-day moving average, and hence, at the end of European trading, I will sell my personal holdings in stocks and move into long-term government bonds.”

Don’t mistake Klement for a perma-bear chasing headlines. He isn’t. Rather, Klement is widely respected and broadly cautious, and notably he conceded that the signal “is not foolproof.”

“While this indicator is not foolproof, market dynamics have turned decisively bearish, in our view. We have consistently warned of an AI bubble since May and have become more bearish since September.”

While the market rallied back above the 200-day average on Thursday, I thought the headline was worth walking through the importance of the 200-day average, as it will happen again, just as it did this past March. That break has been forgotten by the market, but when the Iran crisis erupted, the index broke below the 200-day average for the first time since May 2025. That was when I wrote The 200-DMA Just Broke: What Every Investor Should Know. That analysis found that 4 weeks was critical to deciding what to do next. Fortunately, that break in March only lasted 13 sessions. Six months later, the S&P 500 was 15.8% higher.

The point worth reviewing isn’t whether the 200-day average broke. It’s whether it stays broken.

The Break Started Small. It Didn’t Stay That Way

So, what happened this week that made Klement take action? On November 17, the S&P 500 closed at 7,340.53, four points under its 200-day average at 7,344.53. That ended a run of 155 straight closes above the average that began on April 8. The next session it closed at 7,323.63, just 0.31% below an average that is still rising. By Friday, November 20, it had closed at 6,910.39, 6.0% under the average at 7,348.58. Notice in the chart below that the average climbed all year, including 0.79% over the 20 sessions through November 20.

Such is the problem with treating a single close as a verdict. Everything else deteriorated quickly. The S&P 500 sits 11.6% below its October 6 record of 7,818.93, and the 50-day average is now more than 700 points higher at 7,625.25. The 200-day average tells you the long-term trend is being tested. It doesn’t tell you how the test ends.

One important note as we update the March analysis. Every one of the 34 first breaks since 1950 happened while the long-term average was rising, so its slope describes the setup rather than sorting the “whipsaws” from the real thing. That job falls to time.

Half Of 200-Day Average Breaks Don’t Last Four Weeks

Carson Investment Research circulated a table this week of every first close below the 200-day average after a run of 150 or more days above it. I rebuilt that analysis using Yahoo Finance daily closes, and the figures tie out row for row. (My series starts in January 1950, so the July 1950 signal falls inside the 200-day warmup, leaving 34 completed cases.) However, if we go one step further, we can split them by the question that actually matters. Was the S&P 500 back above its 200-day average 20 trading sessions later?

Eighteen of the 34 were.

Those 18 “failed” breaks turned “sell everything fear” into buying opportunities. The index averaged 4.4% over the following month and was higher in all 18 cases. Twelve months out, the average gain was 14.7% with 88% of cases positive. That’s well ahead of the 9.3% average for any day since 1950.

However, and very importantly, the other 16 tell a different story. When the S&P 500 was still below the 200-day average four weeks later, the average one-month return was −3.5% and the 12-month return was a coin flip. Half were positive. The median was 0.0%.

Here is the problem. When you lump all 34 historical events together, the returns look almost exactly like a random day in the market, which is the whole point. The first close mixes two very different outcomes into one average. The next four weeks tell you which one you’re in.

Depth in the first few sessions has been the tell. All 8 first breaks that ran 2.9% or more below the 200-day average within four sessions were still below it at week four: 1969, 1987, 1990, 1994, 1998, 2011, 2020 and 2025. This break reached 6.0% below the average by its fourth session, on November 20. Every break that went this deep this fast was still below the line a month later.

The Pain Comes Early, And So Does The Whipsaw

Notably, this is where Klement’s rule earns its keep. When the market breaks the 200-day average, and it sticks, the damage comes quickly. Over the next three months, the average maximum drawdown was −8.6%, against −1.9% for breaks that reversed. The worst cases came in 1962, October 1987, and February 2020. Each fell roughly 24% to 25% from the signal close within a year.

So, this is where someone will tell you that’s exactly why you sell on the first close below the 200-day average, and there is merit to that point. Meb Faber’s research on trend-following rules showed a moving-average discipline kept investors out of the worst of the dot-com bust and the financial crisis. However, and this is very critical, Faber’s model only checks the 10-month average once a month. Once a month equals 4 weeks, which filters out breaks below the 200-day average that didn’t stick.

I like Meb’s rule because a daily trigger pays a different toll. In the 18 breaks that reversed, the index closed back above the line within about five sessions. On average, that was 1.6% above where a seller got out. A strict crossover rule then fired another 1.4 sell signals, on average, over the next three months.

As Klement noted, he expects that churn, and that certainly goes to his credit. Bob Farrell’s Rule #8 explains why even real breaks chop: bear markets have three stages, a sharp decline, a reflexive rebound, and a drawn-out fundamental downtrend. In February 2020, the index regained the line two sessions after the break, then fell more than 25% from that rebound within three weeks.

One very important point is that a quick recovery isn’t an “all clear” either. In August 2007, the index was back above the line within a month, topped in October, and was 12.8% lower a year later.

However, here is the one detail that matters most. Measured from the four-week mark, the breaks that stuck still averaged a 9.0% gain over the next year. The breaks that reversed averaged 9.6%. Most of the asymmetry is decided in the first month, which is why the next four weeks matter more than the first close.

“Selling everything on the first close below the 200-day average isn’t risk management. It’s a coin flip with transaction costs.”

What Should Investors Do Now

As we noted last week in VIX Spike: Complacency’s Bill Coming Due, low volatility eventually begets high volatility, and this break fits the pattern. We’re not ignoring the signal, and we’re not liquidating portfolios on the basis of one week of forced selling either. We nibbled on NVDA and PANW as they declined this week. Next week, we will trim value positions to raise cash and reduce market exposure.

Here is the timing. The first market close below the 200-day average was on November 17th. That close started the four-week clock, which expires at the December 16th close. If the S&P 500 is back above its 200-day average by then, history suggests the break was noise rather than a top.

However, if we remain below the 200-day average, the odds shift, and equity exposure needs to adjust accordingly. In the meantime, trimming value positions raises cash without betting on either outcome. The S&P 500 closed below our 7,000 risk line on November 20, at 6,910, which is why that cash raise starts next week.

Klement may well be right about the “AI bubble.” Being right about the bubble and being right about the timing are NOT the same bet. A break of the line can flag the risk, but it takes a month to tell you whether the risk is real.

“So far, this is a valuation and liquidity event, not an earnings recession.”

The first close below the line is rarely where the damage gets done. The next four weeks are.

data.title: Why Your Priciest Stocks Fall First
data.description:
Valuation is a put option. A cheap stock holds up better during multiple compression.

Multiple compression means the market pays less for every $1 of earnings. Rising rates and slowing earnings are driving it now.

Sellers go after the priciest stocks first.

You probably lean on the chart or hide in big names that feel safe.

Don’t get me wrong. Charts matter.

Those companies make big money. Yet neither one tells you what you’re paying.

I’ll show you how I check that with the P/E ratio. You only need a calculator and four quarters of earnings.

The P/E only gets you halfway. You also have to read it against its peers.

My $108,000 account lost $1,200 over three days while the S&P 500 fell 300 points. One futures contract on the index would’ve lost $15,000.

Everything I own has a low multiple.

Let’s start with how multiple compression works. Then I’ll show you the check behind every Genesis COG trade.

How Multiple Compression Works

A multiple is the price you pay for every $1 a company earns. Wall Street calls it the P/E.

Declining earnings and rising interest rates set off multiple compression. Investors start paying less for that same $1.

Bull markets need falling rates and faster growth. Stocks are pricing in a slowdown while bond yields price in inflation.

I call that a bad combo. The Fed’s latest minutes show almost every official expects more rate hikes.

The 30-year Treasury pays about 5.5%. A growth stock with no dividend pays you nothing while you wait.

Earnings beats are slowing to a crawl. Sellers are spreading multiple compression across the whole market.

Jeffrey Gundlach won’t consider the S&P 500 until its P/E falls below 15. The bond king is holding about 30% in stocks.

I agree with him. A 15 multiple would be the buy of the century.

Why Multiple Compression Hits The Priciest Stocks First

The higher the multiple, the harder multiple compression hits the stock.

A multiple of 40 gets me out of a stock. I stay calm at 6x because that multiple works as a floor.

Nvidia (NVDA) sat at 40x when multiple compression started hitting it. It’s already broken.

Drug stocks proved it again this week. Merck (MRK) was down $4.75 on Wednesday when it ran out of buyers.

Bristol Myers (BMY) broke too. GlaxoSmithKline (GSK), the cheapest of the group at about 10x, is down only a fraction.

I own GlaxoSmithKline because it’s cheap.

I’d lighten up on Eli Lilly (LLY) first. It added $269 billion in market value since Oct. 6.

Only Apple (AAPL) added more. I have Lilly at 46x earnings, while its peers trade at 10x to 12x.

I know Lilly is making big money. I’d still fire you if you worked for me and paid 46x for it.

I think it’s the one stock that could break this market.

Why A Low Multiple Works Like A Put

A put option gains value when a stock falls. It works like insurance on the shares you own.

A low multiple does the same job during multiple compression. It limits how far a stock can fall.

Each point on an S&P 500 futures contract is worth $50. That 300-point drop cost $15,000 on one contract.

I kept my loss to $1,200 with three habits.

I’m hedged. No position tops 4%.

Every stock I own also carries a low multiple.

Sellers hit the market for a fifth straight day on Thursday. One futures contract was down $5,000 at one point.

I was down $300 on my $108,000 account.

I didn’t always trade this way. I was Mr. Momentum 20 years ago.

I was up 30% one year and lost 30% the next. I blew my accounts out.

I’ve made more mistakes over 38 years than all of you combined.

Valuation is a put option. Everything I buy starts with it.

The Check Behind Every Genesis COG Trade

I run three steps to gauge multiple compression risk before I buy:

  1. Add up four quarters. Total the last four quarters of earnings. Divide that into the share price.

  2. Read it against the peers. Check what similar companies trade for.

  3. Let the chart pick the day. I don’t buy on the way down, no matter how cheap.

Williams-Sonoma (WSM) is a $230 stock. Its last four quarters add up to close to $10.

That’s about 22x earnings. I won’t pay that with housing in a bear market.

That bear market could drag it into multiple compression.

Marvell (MRVL) came out at 45x on a calculator I borrowed from my daughter. The semiconductor I bought that day trades at 11x.

I like my chances of multiple expansion better.

I track about 40 bank stocks. Only Wells Fargo (WFC) trades cheaper than U.S. Bancorp (USB), the one I own.

The chart only tells me when. Value comes first.

Stuff that’s cheap always comes back.

Every Genesis COG trade follows that order.

The model picks the timing only after the value checks out. It never buys in a downward channel.

I’m holding 55% cash right now. I won’t force a trade to put it to work.

USD/CAD

The United States dollar continues to rally against the Canadian dollar as it has broken above the 1.43 level and is now threatening a major area of noise between 1.43 and 1.45. Short-term pullbacks continue to be a potential buying opportunity, but at this juncture, the one thing that seems to be driving this market more than anything else will be the interest rate differential between the United States and Canada.

Furthermore, the Canadian market has to deal with oil being fairly soft, and of course, the market makes a certain amount of sense that the overall attitude of this is still one that there are plenty of buyers waiting to get involved and take advantage of value as it occurs.

EUR/USD

The euro has broken below the crucial 1.10 level, an area that's a large, round, psychologically significant figure and an area that a lot of people will be watching. After that, we could be looking at the 1.08 level. Short-term rallies, I think, open up the possibility of shorting opportunities at the first signs of exhaustion.

The euro has to worry about the interest rate differential favoring the United States, but also has to worry about energy problems overall. After all, the Europeans may have some issues when it comes to procuring energy over the winter.

Gold

The gold market has absolutely gotten crushed during the week, and it finds itself sitting just above the crucial $3,500 level. The $3,500 level is an area that a lot of people will be watching due to the previous resistance barrier from trading back in the early part of 2025.

There's no sign of life here in the gold market, and as long as the real rates continue to be positive in the United States, it makes non-yielding assets such as gold much less attractive. This is a horrible-looking chart, and I suspect rallies at this point in time will end up being potential selling opportunities at the first signs of serious trouble.

Silver

The silver markets have collapsed as well, as they are sitting just above the $41 level heading into the weekend and, quite frankly, can't seem to catch a bid. We sliced through the $45 level, and the previous week even broke down below the $50 level for the third time in a month.

Ultimately, the market is one that is looking for some signs of hope out there, but unfortunately, as long as those real rates are positive, silver is an absolute disaster waiting to happen. Longer term, I like silver, but ultimately there's no sign of life here.

WTI Crude Oil

The WTI crude oil market fell during the week as well, breaking down below the 61.8% Fibonacci retracement level from the move back in July. The 50-week EMA is in the same neighborhood, and it looks like the market is trying to respect $80 as a floor.

We continue to have a lot of questions asked about the supply of crude oil, but we also have to keep in mind that there are still tensions that could cause issues in the Middle East, and while it doesn't directly affect the WTI market, the carry-on effect could cause issues.

DAX

The DAX in Germany looks absolutely horrible. The candlestick for the week was absolutely brutal, and it looks like we are threatening the 24,500 level. The size of the candlestick is quite shocking, and if we see continuation to the downside, the next major support level is closer to the 23,500 level, possibly the 22,000 level.

If the market were to rally from here, it could, in theory, at least stay in the same range that it had been in, but this is one of the poorest-looking candlesticks for the week as Germany continues to worry about energy and, quite frankly, the ECB is somewhat noncommittal as to its monetary policy.

NASDAQ 100

The Nasdaq 100 has collapsed as well for the week, and it looks like we simply don't have any real support at the moment, as there are still plenty of concerns about the AI trade and everything that's going on with NVIDIA (NVDA).

Overall, I do think eventually this market turns around, but those higher rates and the nonsense coming out of the NVIDIA investigations that paint the AI market in a certain light have been disastrous for the Nasdaq. Ultimately, I think rallies end up being selling opportunities, with the $23,000 level possibly the floor in the market.

Bitcoin

The Bitcoin market (BTC.X) has broken down rather significantly as well, as we are now below the $60.000 level and testing major support going back to 2024. Quite frankly, in an environment where something like the Nasdaq can't get a bid, it's hard to imagine how Bitcoin would.

Bitcoin looks horrible. I believe at this point in time any rally that we get is likely going to be sold into at the first signs of exhaustion. Bitcoin remains very bearish.

data.title: WTI Crude Oil Rebounds Toward $85 As Middle East Risks Loom Ahead Of Thanksgiving
data.description:
Liquid Gold remains locked in the mindsets of global traders. As equity indices turn in sour results in most major markets, the price of energy is another constant reminder that sentiment is being stirred by fragile conditions. The price of WTI Crude Oil turned in a fascinating couple of days trading before going into the weekend. Whispers persist of increasing tensions in the Middle East. The main actors including the U.S and Iran have been heightening signals that another military escalation may be drawing close. In the meantime, day traders need to continue to read the tea leaves carefully.

Middle East Tensions Cloud WTI’s Thanksgiving Week Outlook

After falling with sincere velocity early on Friday morning, WTI Crude Oil started to see increased buying around the halfway point and went into the weekend within sight of the weekly high. However, more importantly perhaps, is the sound of war drums that has started to be heard again from the U.S and the Middle East.

While some analysts continue to try and talk the price of WTI Crude Oil lower with optimistic words of a peace accord somehow being negotiated, rumblings from Iran and the U.S should keep all WTI Crude Oil traders ready for a different set of results. The U.S is going into a long holiday weekend because of the Thanksgiving holiday this coming Thursday, so perhaps there will be perception that quiet will prevail for a handful of days. This should make the short and near-term volatile as large players try to position themselves ahead of a possible storm.

WTI Rebounds From Nearly $82 but Closes Below $85

Yes, WTI Crude Oil went into the weekend below $85.00, and this is lower than the previous Friday’s close. Yet news of renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Houthis via rockets, oil tankers in the Hormuz Strait having problems, and missile attacks on Bahrain from Iran, should make WTI Crude Oil traders anxious. Preparing for the potential of heightened conflict between Iran and the U.S may prove important. After hitting a low of nearly $82.00 on early Friday, WTI Crude Oil started to reverse higher.

Looking for support below to ignite buying positions may remain a worthwhile bet in the coming days, but tomorrow’s opening if prices remain near Friday’s close and go higher may signal nervousness has crept upwards this weekend among large players. Retail speculators are at the mercy of momentum caused by folks who are not only looking at supply ratios and logistical statistics from the Middle East, but by perceptions military escalation threatens.

Pre-Thanksgiving Positioning Could Amplify Oil Price Swings

The notion that higher prices in WTI Crude Oil act as an ‘insurance policy’ of sorts by large players as they price in elevated risks is logical. And with a marketplace that will lose a considerable amount of trading volume by this coming Wednesday, day traders need to understand that large players may be inclined to price in their nervous sentiment before leaving for a long holiday weekend.

While trading will take place late this week, volumes could become untrustworthy and create volatility that can harm day traders who are simply looking to bet on directions. Meaning that trading early this week may see increased action caused by large players who may be ultra-active and cause fluctuations in an already nervous marketplace.

Could WTI Resume Its Decline if Military Escalation Is Avoided?

Having fallen to nearly $82.00 on Friday, some optimistic traders may be inclined to bet against the noise and believe lower prices in WTI Crude Oil will prevail. The closing price of nearly $84.84 this Friday can be taken in a very positive light. There is a chance large players may not believe military escalation will take this week and that the price of WTI Crude Oil should drop further. Looking for potential quick hitting moves chasing support technical support levels may prove possible for retail traders.

Oil Traders Face Geopolitical Risks and Broader Market Nerves

data.title: U.S. Stocks: Look Out Above
data.description:
Week 48 | Outlook: 23–27 November 2026

This week the S&P 500 and Dow joined the Nasdaq in correction territory, with Friday’s brutal selling accelerating into the close, leaving many to ponder which fund(s) had blown up. The S&P (SPX) lost 3.70% on the day and 8.61% on the week, while the Nasdaq Composite (NDX) fell 5.61% on Friday and just over 10% for the week. We think the set up offers scope for a sharp rebound well worth playing for, but the form the bounce takes deserves monitoring closely.

Strong earnings results weren’t enough to change the bearish mood among investors. Nvidia (NVDA) reported quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion and forecast approximately $130 billion for the following quarter, yet its shares continued to freefall. Anthropic’s much anticipated flotation also failed to restore confidence across technology. We believe investors are becoming more demanding about what they’ll pay for future growth, especially where financing, export access and corporate governance complicate the story. A healthy order book doesn’t make the share price inexpensive.

Nor has the retreat produced a uniform rush into defensive assets. Treasuries strengthened, with the ten-year yield reported near 4.91% late on Friday afternoon, while gold remained under pressure. Oil recovered from its earlier Friday losses but still finished another week lower. We think that combination points towards a growing concern about growth and liquidity, rather than a simple inflation trade in which tangible assets rise together. Gold’s failure to benefit from falling bond yields is particularly difficult to ignore.

There is a credible case against assuming the economy is already falling apart. Our macro composite score remains mixed at 54.4 out of 100, and the latest initial unemployment claims release showed 203,000 claims, only a modest increase. Nvidia's results were good. However, with the selling we saw our equity breadth score has weakened to 32.2 and sentiment has fallen to 15.8, classified as extreme fear. We think those readings make a short term rebound in equities more than plausible, and it is likely to be a strong rally.

Most of this week's potential catalysts arrive on Wednesday 25 November, but we wouldn't wait for results to get long. October personal income and outlays, including PCE inflation, arrive alongside the second estimate of third-quarter GDP at 13:30 GMT. Durable goods orders are due at the same time, followed by new home sales at 15:00 and the Fed’s Beige Book at 19:00. HPE’s Monday evening call, followed by Dell (DELL) and Workday (WDAY) on Tuesday evening, gives investors another look at enterprise technology demand. Thanksgiving makes this an unusual five session outlook. US cash equities are closed on Thursday 26 November and finish at 18:00 GMT on Friday 27 November.

US indices: odds favour the bulls this week

The reported positioning change runs from Tuesday 10 November to Tuesday 17 November. Leveraged funds added 52,078 E-mini S&P 500 longs and covered 16,004 shorts, improving their net position by 68,082 contracts. They nevertheless remained net short by 234,978 contracts. That is a substantial reduction in bearish exposure during a falling market, but not a move into an outright net long position. We think that distinction makes this report less reassuring than a casual reading might suggest.

Funds had already used part of their capacity to cover shorts before the subsequent sell-off accelerated. There are still plenty of shorts outstanding, but the report doesn’t show an untouched reservoir of pessimism suddenly waiting to reverse. Our Wednesday–Friday inference is that the renewed selling probably rebuilt some bearish exposure and discouraged the fresh longs added earlier. Monday and Tuesday could still alter that direction before the next positioning observation. Thanksgiving delays publication of that next COT report until Monday 30 November.

The five-year SPY seasonal profile offers a more supportive counterweight. Across 2021–2025, the Week 48 average return was approximately 1.13%, and the seasonal path rises through this part of November. That gives us a reason to take a recovery attempt seriously. Current breadth and sentiment readings support that view. The deterioration has now extended beyond the largest technology shares, and while relatively stronger performance elsewhere can make an equal-weight comparison look encouraging, losing less than the market leader is useful resilience but isn’t the same as broad buying. A decent bounce followed by a retest of the recent lows to give us a breadth washout would be a better marker of a lasting low.

With the sell off emanating from tech, we thought we would take a look at the Nasdaq 100 ETF (QQQ) for a steer on the chances of a recovery. Friday sell offs of 5%+ are quite rare, and in all cases bar the second year of the dot-com bear market we saw sizeable returns over the following week. That is our base case for this week then, but be warned that a lack of upside follow through early on would be an omen of something far more bearish about to play out. For QQQ we have support at 593.86, with resistance at 631.45, 650.90 then 706.64. For SPY we have support at 671.38, with resistance at 723.07 and 740.71.

Gold: much unloved but worth watching

Gold’s Tuesday-to-Tuesday report, covering 10–17 November, shows managed money reducing its net long by 9,399 contracts to 102,942. Long holdings fell by 5,412 contracts while shorts increased by 3,987. The resulting position sits at the 44th percentile of its own 4 year history. Enthusiasm has been reduced, but this is neither a net short market nor an extreme positioning washout. Unfortunately we think there is still room for investors to reduce exposure if the metal continues to disappoint when protection is most wanted.

The Wednesday–Friday inference is for further erosion of that net long. Gold weakened after Tuesday, Thursday’s early recovery failed to establish a durable improvement, and Friday brought renewed pressure even as Treasuries rallied. We think the most likely positioning consequence is continued retreat from bullish exposure. Gold's inability to respond to lower nominal yields suggests that concern about Fed policy is offsetting it's usual defensive appeal.

Seasonality argues against becoming too comfortable with the downside. GLD’s five-year Week 48 average is approximately +1.56%, and its seasonal path improves into late November. We think that raises the chance of a rebound this week in tandem with stocks. Since gold has already failed to deliver the protection that fearful equity sentiment might have suggested, we can assume it now trades in lock-step with equities instead.

Our preferred view is a hesitant start followed by an attempt to stabilise around Wednesday’s inflation release. Softer inflation and a less demanding dollar backdrop would give that recovery a good foundation. We don’t yet expect an immediate return to the earlier uptrend and see a bounce this week as the prelude to further lows ahead. Resistance in GLD is 339.83 with support at 293.70 to 305.63.

Oil: a bounce into a challenging fundamental backdrop

Managed money’s WTI position became more defensive between Tuesday 10 and Tuesday 17 November. Funds added 5,519 longs, but added a much larger 15,419 shorts. The net long consequently fell by 9,900 contracts to just 15,814. Positioning sits at the 7.7th percentile of its own history. This was a change driven by heavier short additions, rather than an across-the-board liquidation of long holdings, and it leaves oil much closer to the pessimistic end of its range than gold.

Our Wednesday–Friday inference is that the week’s renewed weakness probably encouraged further defensive positioning, although Friday’s recovery may have whipsawed the new shorts. Oil’s final session was firmer than the early reports suggested, and gives oil bulls some hope to cling to, but the broader weekly direction remained down. Reports of stronger Middle Eastern exports are weighing against the disruption premium, while Saturday’s fresh report of a tanker strike near Hormuz underlines how quickly the balance can change. We would not treat either additional supply promises or a single incident as proof of an effect on physical deliveries. Definitive supply has become harder to gauge.

The five year USO seasonal pattern is much less friendly than the other three markets. Its Week 48 average return was approximately −0.44%, and the surrounding late-November path is uneven and generally weak. Together with deteriorating risk appetite, that makes us reluctant to interpret the Friday rebound as the start of a new advance. While the net-long positioning is low historically, there is room to drop further and we feel the short term bear case is stronger on balance.

We expect a volatile opening, with weekend shipping headlines capable of extending Friday’s recovery quite sharply. Our preferred path is for that strength to struggle as attention returns to exports, demand and Wednesday’s economic releases, leaving oil vulnerable again into the holiday period. That is a modest bearish preference, not a forecast of an ouright freefall. Resistance in USO stands at 144.90 and 164.67, with support at 138.01 then 124.68.

US bonds: protection comes with crowded positioning

Asset managers increased their net long in US ten-year Treasury futures by 117,073 contracts between Tuesday 10 and Tuesday 17 November, reaching 3,270,834. They added 180,449 longs and 63,376 shorts. The net position stands at the 100th percentile of the recorded historical comparison. This is genuinely a large positive net position, unlike the still-negative S&P stance. We think it provides evidence of substantial institutional commitment to duration, while also warning that an unwinding could result in a sharp decline.

Our Wednesday–Friday inference is that the later Treasury rally probably reinforced that commitment. The strongest defensive response came as equity selling intensified on Friday, and the reported ten-year yield fell to approximately 4.91% late in the afternoon. That is a price observation after the COT cutoff, not evidence that Tuesday’s reported position already captured the rally. We think the next report is more likely to show continued support for duration than a wholesale retreat, unless the first two sessions of the coming week sharply reverse the move.

IEF’s five-year seasonal profile supports the near-term bond case, with a Week 48 average return of approximately +1.39%. Fearful equity sentiment provides another source of demand. The main obstacle is policy: the October Fed minutes, released this week, still described further rate increases as likely appropriate under participants’ baseline outlooks. We believe Wednesday’s inflation figures will further test whether defensive buying can offset that threat.

On balance this week we expect bonds to decline in the face of an equity market bounce that should prompt some profit taking after Friday’s move. A strong inflation release could result in that decline gathering speed. For IEF resistance stands at 92.03, with supprt at 89.95 then 88.52 and 87.78.

Our next article will be published on Sunday. Until then, we wish you well for the week ahead. If you have any questions about anything covered here, please get in touch. We’re always happy to hear from you.

data.title: The S&P 500 Breaks Major Technical Support As Nvidia Drags It Down
data.description:
The S&P 500 had a rough week, finishing down about 8.5%, and the Nasdaq finished down about 10.5%. Even after that, the S&P 500 is only about 6% below its 200-day moving average, and it was last in this range in March. In previous corrective phases, the index has gotten a lot lower, about 13% below in April 2025, about 17% in the 2022 bear market, and about 25% during COVID.

So if this is a deeper correction, there might still be a little further to go. If this is just a sharp V-shaped recovery, then we have probably gone far enough to satisfy it. The only issue I see with a V-shaped recovery is that Nvidia (NVDA) is the key to this, and right now there are lots of questions around Nvidia.

From an options standpoint, Nvidia could keep falling because there isn’t much support until the put wall. The SMH closed Friday right around its put wall, about 23% off its 200-day moving average, and for the S&P 500 the put wall is quite a distance below Friday’s close. The option market and the technical charts align here. If we do not get a rally to start the day on Monday, there could be a little more air underneath us before the market starts finding a floor.

I also built a model that tracks where systematic flows are headed, and it suggests potential for more systematic selling in the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq. Systematic funds don’t look at fundamentals. Rates have come down a little, but they are still higher than they were on November 6, so we are not getting a full flight to safety yet.

The AUD/JPY is one of the risk gauges I like to watch closely. Its relationship with the VIX has turned positive more recently, and now it is returning to its more inverse nature; the same is happening with the S&P 500. This perhaps suggests global de-risking, with some of the carry trades of the last couple of years beginning to unwind, rates in Japan higher, and the loss of the AI trade in Nvidia.

If the sell-off continues, it creates a bit of a problem for the Fed. The financial conditions index I built has tightened a lot over the last couple of days, and if that continues, it will limit how much the Fed can raise rates, because tighter conditions are doing the job for the Fed. It is early for that, and it is more about conditions staying tight for a while. That is what happened in 2015 and 2016, when the Fed raised rates in late 2015, conditions continued to tighten, and it eventually had to back off.

The VIX closed around 36 on Friday, and my VIX model suggests it should be higher than where it is, based on correlations and single-stock volatility. During the 2022 bear market, it inverted and stayed that way until March 2023. If this indicator stays below or near zero for a prolonged period, it could mean the market is assigning all the risk to single stocks rather than the broader index, and that we could be in a longer pullback. Right now we don’t have that signal, but it is worth watching over the next couple of weeks.

data.title: A S&P 500 Thanksgiving Rally May Be No Match For This Week’s Liquidity Squeeze
data.description:
It will be a shortened holiday week for the S&P 500, but that doesn’t mean it won’t be important, especially after last week’s sharp sell-off. Perhaps most importantly, the market will get the all-important October PCE report on Wednesday. Headline PCE is expected to rise by 0.3% month over month, down from 0.5% in September, while increasing by 3.8% year over year, up from 3.6% in September. Core PCE is expected to rise by 0.3% month over month, matching September’s pace, while climbing by 3.2% year over year, up from 3.1% in September.

On top of that, this will be a big week for Treasury settlements, with $51.3 billion settling on Tuesday, followed by $28 billion in coupon securities and $16.6 billion in Treasury bills on November 27. With net issuance likely to continue rising through the week of December 7, risk assets are likely to feel the pinch. Bitcoin (BTC.X) certainly has, as it has been testing a break below $60,000 and now faces the risk of a further decline toward $54,000.

Periods of heavy Treasury issuance also tend to coincide with rising implied volatility, and this period has been no different. The 1-day VIX climbed to 51 on Friday, suggesting there is a good chance of a volatility crush on Monday. With the holiday-shortened trading week, implied volatility should fall sharply, potentially helping stocks rally. The question is whether those mechanical forces can overcome the liquidity pressures created by Treasury issuance, even during a shortened trading week. Certainly, Tuesday’s settlement day, along with Wednesday morning’s PCE report, argues against that continuing past Monday.

The bigger issue is that any volatility crush is likely to be short-lived, given the high-stakes PCE report on Wednesday. That means implied volatility will probably start to rise again on Tuesday ahead of the report. The biggest question this week is which force will prevail: liquidity pressures or mechanical forces. Given how the market has performed recently, one would think liquidity pressures would win out. The problem is that positioning has become so stretched that it’s difficult to bet against a sharp snapback rally.

In fact, the current heat map of implied volatility and skew shows the top 50 stocks in the S&P 500 clustered in the upper-left corner. At this point, the options market is about as bearish as it can get.

The main difference between this year’s Thanksgiving period and last year is that the circumstances surrounding Nvidia (NVDA) and the broader AI trade are entirely different. Ultimately, if volatility sellers fail to show up this week, it could be a very long week for the markets. With both the VIX and realized volatility at such elevated levels, it seems unlikely that volatility sellers will step in aggressively. On top of that, CTA positioning suggests these strategies are likely to be sellers as well, which could make for a particularly challenging week for stocks.

My best guess is that any bounce we see on Monday, driven by the volatility unwind following last Friday’s close, is unlikely to last beyond Monday. From there, the rest of the holiday-shortened trading week could turn into a back-and-forth battle between liquidity pressures and mechanical forces.
