data.title: Stock Market Next Week: Can Stocks And The Euro Fall Further?
data.description:
Can stocks and the euro fall further next week? Yes, and the Fed will not rescue the stock market the way it did in 2019. I expect the Nasdaq 100 to lose another 10% from Friday's close of 25,029, to about 22,500, in the coming weeks, dollar funding strain to keep building, first outside the United States, and the euro to keep falling toward $1.08. Next week's speed depends on Asia's open on Monday: a slow grind below Friday's low of 24,910, toward 24,000, if Asia holds, gaps toward 22,500 if it panics. Rebounds, and history says there will likely be some, are where I would sell again.

This was the Nasdaq 100's worst week since March 2020: it lost 10.43% to 25,028.98, including a 5.61% fall on Friday, and stands 19.8% below its October 6 record. The S&P 500 lost 8.61% to 6,910.39 and chip stocks 17.1%; their index has closed below its 200-day moving average every day since October 30, after 355 sessions above it. The VIX, the implied volatility of the S&P 500 over the next 30 days, went from 19.30 to 35.89, its highest close of the past year. Gold fell 8.9% to $3,538, the 10 year Treasury yield 19 basis points (hundredths of a percentage point) to 4.94%, and the euro closed at $1.0968, a hair above Thursday's closing low of the year.

What I wrote, and what the market did

First, what did not work. On November 6 I called the rebound a dead cat bounce and wrote that a close above 27,270 on the Nasdaq 100 would prove me wrong. It closed at 27,907.63 on November 9, and the fall came a week later than I had written.

On November 14 I wrote: "I don't expect a Santa rally before the Fed meeting of December 9, and if the Fed is still hawkish, there will be no Fed put to support stocks." Since then the S&P 500 has lost 8.6%, and fed funds futures still price a hike on December 9.

The same day, on the euro: "The euro keeps falling against the dollar." It went from $1.1023 to $1.0968. I added: "For EUR/JPY to fall in earnest, USD/JPY has to stop rising." USD/JPY slipped from 159.71 to 158.57, and EUR/JPY fell 1.24% to 173.92, more than against the dollar.

On October 30: "Bonds hedge again, gold does not." This week gold lost 8.9%, to its lowest close of the past year, while the 10 year Treasury yield fell 19 basis points. Stocks and yields now fall together, and gold is sold for cash: a liquidity sell-off, not a flight to safety.

Can the Nasdaq fall another 10%?

Yes. The Nasdaq 100 closed Friday 10.8% below its 200-day moving average of 28,073, the line between a correction in an uptrend and a downtrend. On my Bloomberg, more than half of its members stand at least 20% below their 52-week high. Another 10% would take it to about 22,500, below its March 30 close of 22,953, the low of the past year. Support: Friday's intraday low of 24,910, then 24,000. Resistance: 26,450, between Friday's high and Thursday's close, then 27,000 to 27,600, where it closed from Monday to Wednesday before losing it on Thursday.

What pushes. The sellers come in layers, and none of them has finished.

  • Trend followers (CTAs, funds that buy what rises and sell what falls) are already short: on our terminal, CTA positioning in US equities stood at about minus $20 billion at Friday's close, after flipping from long to short in November.

  • Hedge funds have cut their net bets but not their gross leverage: unwinding it means selling the crowded AI longs. CFTC data for the week to Tuesday, before the worst of the fall, show it: leveraged funds swung by 24,895 contracts to a net short of 10,928 E-mini Nasdaq 100 futures, while covering 68,082 contracts of their short in S&P 500 futures. The bet is against tech, not against the whole market.

  • Volatility-targeting funds (vol control, risk parity) keep their risk constant, so they sell stocks when volatility rises, and bonds too if funding strain lifts yields.

  • Leveraged ETFs, most of them on tech, sell into the close on big down days.

  • Dealers, the market's plumbing, carried about $97 billion of Treasury bills on November 11, in the top fifth of their two-year range. If funding tightens, they quote less, and a correction gaps.

  • Credit now feeds equity. High yield spreads, the extra yield junk bonds pay over Treasuries, widened 51 basis points to 367, and those of the riskiest tier, rated Caa, 91 to 1,174, both one-year highs. CoreWeave's five year credit default swap, the price of insuring its debt, ended at 1,291 basis points, also a one-year high. On Friday CoreWeave lost 12.0%, Nebius 16.1%, Nvidia 14.0% and Oracle 8.5%, and Anthropic, which raised the most money ever for a new share issue (private placement included), lost 8.5% and ended Friday less than $6 above its offering price. The AI buildout is now testing how much money markets can supply: on Thursday SpaceX priced about $32 billion of bonds, arranged by Goldman Sachs and Apollo, through a vehicle that buys Nvidia chips and leases them to SpaceX, and the part sold to corporate bond buyers had to pay about 100 basis points more than SpaceX's own bonds of similar maturity sold earlier this year.

What brakes. Companies buying back their own shares, now out of their blackout, are the largest buyer against the fall. Pension funds rebalance into stocks after a drop, a bid that fades under stress. Asset managers rotate into quality, not the Nasdaq: this week the equal weight S&P 500 lost about 6.2%, against 8.6% for the index and 12.5% for technology stocks, while consumer staples, at a record close on Monday, lost 2.1%. On Thursday my colleague Lucas Erbrech, of the CrossVol Derivatives Team, looked at where to hide if the AI trade breaks. Part of the trend-following selling has already happened. There is no capitulation yet, so the flush that usually ends a fall is still ahead. All these sellers share one circuit breaker: a fall deep enough to exhaust the trend followers and push the Fed to its balance sheet.

Confirmation: a close below 24,910, then 24,000, or another credit event at a neocloud, an AI cloud renter such as CoreWeave or Nebius. Invalidation: a close back above 26,450 that holds, with a Fed that signals a pause in December.

What happens in Asia on Monday?

Asia has to absorb Friday's fall in New York first, and that decides the speed: Tokyo, Seoul and Taipei had closed before it. In New York on Friday, Taiwan Semiconductor's shares lost 9.5%, the Taiwan and Korea ETFs 11.0% and 8.4%, and Nikkei futures in Chicago settled 3.3% below Tokyo's close. Asian investors are still heavily invested in AI and semiconductors. Taiwan's Taiex already lost 17.5% this week, and Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission has tightened again after a first round on November 9. From Friday, a stock that closes down 3.5% or more cannot be sold short below its previous close the next day. On Saturday it extended the ban to all listed stocks from Monday, raised the minimum margin on short sales from 130% to 150% and suspended new listings of put warrants.

In Japan, I am wary of SoftBank. Its shares lost 14.5% on Friday to ¥3,025, the lowest close of the past year, 65% below their June 2 high. ARM, the chip designer whose shares back SoftBank's financing, then lost 14.1% in New York after Tokyo had closed. On September 25 I wrote: "The collateral chains are circular. SoftBank's margin loan is secured on ARM shares." That is my weak point to watch: ARM in New York on Monday, then SoftBank on Tuesday, when Tokyo reopens after a public holiday.

So my base case for the week is conditional. If Asia does not panic at the open, I expect a slow, choppy grind lower on the Nasdaq 100, below Friday's low of 24,910 and toward 24,000. If it does panic, the fall goes faster, with gaps, toward my 10%. The first answer comes on Monday at 1:00 a.m. Paris time, when Seoul opens, then Taipei at 2:00. Japan's markets are closed on Monday for Labor Thanksgiving Day, a public holiday, so Tokyo only answers on Tuesday, at the same hour.

Are investors hedging?

Yes, judging by option prices: close to the money and for the next few days. The VVIX, the volatility of the VIX, which rises when investors pay up for VIX calls, went from 101.53 to 138.03, above its November 5 crash level and far above the 121 of October 16. The VIX curve inverted from the short end: 40.72 for the 9-day VIX, 35.89 for the 30-day, 30.94 for the 3-month. The 1-day VIX closed at 51.34, a one standard deviation move of about 3.2% priced for Monday alone.

On my Bloomberg's volatility surface (3:50 p.m. New York time), four week implied volatility on S&P 500 options 1.5% below the index doubled between the two Fridays, from 16.5% to 33.8%, while puts 10% below went from 26.5% to 43.1%, a smaller rise. The Cboe SKEW index, a gauge of how expensive far out of the money puts are, fell every day of the week, from 147.14 to 138.84. And some were still selling volatility: in the week to Tuesday, leveraged funds added 38,154 contracts to their net short in VIX futures, to 72,916, just before the VIX jumped. Investors hedging at the money expect a move, not a collapse. On October 18 I wrote: "The VIX woke up on Friday, and it woke up loaded the other way."

Is there a dollar funding problem?

Not yet in the United States, but it is building outside, and that is the second part of my view. In the US, the plumbing is tight, not broken. The Fed's reverse repo facility, the cushion where money funds parked spare cash, held $0.4 billion on Friday, so every new Treasury bill now draws on bank reserves ($3.0 trillion on Wednesday). SOFR, the main overnight repo rate, printed 3.91% on Thursday, 1 basis point above the 3.90% the Fed pays on reserves, after 3.97% at the start of the month. The Fed's standing repo facility, the emergency door at 4.00%, lent $1 million on Friday, and the swap lines with the ECB and the Bank of Japan are almost unused.

One leveraged position keeps growing: in the week to Tuesday, leveraged funds added 181,116 contracts to their short in 10 year Treasury note futures and 52,916 in ultra long bond futures, while covering 2 and 5 year. That is the futures leg of the basis trade, funded in repo, and it keeps moving to the long end, as I wrote on September 22 in The Basis Trade Did Not Shrink Its Risk. It Moved It to the Long End.

Outside, the strain is visible. I could not read the cross-currency basis, the direct price of borrowing dollars against euros, on Friday (minus 3.6 basis points at the end of October, when I wrote that French stress had reached dollar funding), so I use interbank funding. Three month Euribor, the rate at which banks lend each other euros, closed 23.2 basis points above the three month €STR swap, the expected overnight rate, against 17.5 a week earlier and about 11 in late September. In Tokyo, three month TIBOR stands 46.4 basis points above its overnight swap, against 41.4. In India, the central bank accepted none of the 81 bids at a six month bill auction on November 4; the next two auctions were fully accepted, but one year bills yield 113 basis points above the policy rate. China's factory index fell to 49.3 in October, below the 50 line. Brazil's main stock index closed Thursday 20.4% below its October 9 record (Friday was a holiday there). Foreign central banks' Treasury holdings at the New York Fed fell on November 11 to $2.52 trillion, the lowest since October 2010, and recovered $20 billion a week later.

Signs the squeeze has reached New York: SOFR more than 5 basis points above the effective fed funds rate, weaker Treasury auctions ($183 billion of notes next week), the standing repo facility used in size, and the French spread over Germany back above its October 22 closing peak of 174 basis points (157 on Friday).

Can the euro fall to 1.08?

Yes, I expect it to get there. EUR/USD closed below 1.10 every day this week and ended at $1.0968. Below 1.0950, my next levels are 1.0913, 1.0880 and 1.08.

The rate gap did not push it this week: markets price a 92% chance of a Fed hike on December 9 and 91% for the ECB on December 17, and the two year gap between Treasury and German yields narrowed from 171.6 to 158.8 basis points. What pushes the euro lower is the demand for dollars in a sell-off, and France: its 10 year spread over Germany widened to 157 basis points, it pays 47 more than Italy, and S&P is scheduled to review its rating on Friday. One month implied volatility on EUR/USD is only 6.13%: FX options are still calm.

Positioning is the risk. Speculators held a net short of 142,710 euro futures contracts on Tuesday, November 17. Apart from the two previous reports, of October 27 and November 3, it has not been this large since January 2016.

A crowded short is not a squeeze on its own: it needs a catalyst, and a hawkish ECB on December 17 could be one. My views also have one friction: a US crash deep enough to break the labor market would take the Fed's hike off the table, and with it the dollar's main support. Then the euro would stop around 1.08 to 1.09. My euro call works best in an orderly decline, not in a crash.

Will the Fed rescue stocks like in 2019?

No. The comparison everyone makes this week is the autumn of 2018. On November 20, 2018, the S&P 500 stood 9.9% below its September record. It lost another 11.0% into Christmas Eve, and the rebound held once the Fed turned, in January 2019. This year it closed Friday 11.6% below its October 6 record: a similar distance, in the same season. But on October 13 I also wrote: "That analogue needs a Fed that turns." This Fed has no reason to turn.

In 2018 the Fed could turn at no cost: inflation was at target and growth was slowing. Today core PCE inflation is 3.1%, core consumer prices rise 0.3% a month, and growth runs at 3.4% annualized. The Fed's staff blames tariffs, energy and the AI buildout itself. Cutting now would look like surrender.

The committee says it in its own words. On October 28 it held the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4.00%, and two members voted for a hike. The minutes, published on Wednesday, say that "almost all participants judged" that further action to raise rates "would likely be appropriate". They also say that almost all participants discussed the risk that "the returns on AI investment turned out to be disappointing to investors". The Fed sees the AI risk and has decided that inflation comes first.

If the sell-off goes on, the repricing runs down one rung at a time. Fed funds futures price 0.92 of a quarter point hike on December 9, against 1.06 a week earlier, when a small chance of a half point was also in the price. The half point is gone. Next comes a pause. A cut needs new information: payrolls that break, oil that falls hard (Brent is at $92.57), a funding accident.

Support, if it comes, will come from the balance sheet: the New York Fed can buy Treasury bills to keep reserves ample (zero in October, decided month by month). That calms repo and short rates, not the Nasdaq.

How far can a rebound go?

History says a rebound is likely, and that in markets this volatile it was more often a chance to sell than the start of a recovery. Since 1985 the Nasdaq 100 has had 30 weeks like this one, a fall of 10% or more over five sessions (counting at most one per month). In 24 of them it was already as volatile as now, with typical daily moves above 2.2% over the previous month (2.4% today). In those 24 episodes:

  • One week later, the index was higher 15 times, by a median of 1.8%.

  • Within two weeks, its best close was at least 5% above the starting point 17 times, and the median best close was 7.0% higher.

  • One month later, it was higher only 13 times (median +0.9%), and below its best close of the first two weeks 15 times, by a median of 5.1 percentage points.

  • Along the way, it closed below the starting level at some point in 18 of the 24 episodes, a median of 6.4% lower.

From Friday's 25,029, a 5% to 7% rebound would take the Nasdaq 100 to about 26,280 to 26,780, into the 26,450 resistance and toward the 27,000 to 27,600 zone it lost on Thursday. A 6.4% fall from Friday would take it to about 23,430.

What could trigger a rebound next week?

This week investors bought puts close to the money, and the dealers who sold them hedged by selling futures. As I explained on November 14 in No Santa Rally Before the Fed, when implied volatility falls those puts lose delta, the hedge becomes too big and dealers buy futures back: a vanna rally. Time does the same over a long weekend. With the 1-day VIX at 51, any session that passes without a shock can start one. The catalysts on the calendar:

  • Monday, Asia's open. If Seoul and Taipei absorb Friday's fall in New York without panic, on the first day of Taiwan's wider short-sale ban, implied volatility can drop fast. That is the first and most likely trigger. Tokyo, closed on Monday for a public holiday, follows on Tuesday. Asia also has its own hawks this week: Bloomberg Economics expects a rate hike in South Korea, and Tokyo inflation that supports a December hike by the Bank of Japan. The US sells 2 year notes the same day (5 year on Tuesday, 7 year on Wednesday, $183 billion in all).

  • Until Saturday, November 28, when the Fed's quiet period before its December 8-9 meeting starts: any Fed official who opens the door to a pause.

  • Wednesday: October PCE inflation, the second estimate of third quarter GDP and jobless claims, a day early. A soft PCE print would trim the 92% chance of a December hike, but it is not the base case: Bloomberg Economics expects headline PCE prices up 0.32% in October, taking the yearly rate to 3.8% from 3.6%.

  • Thursday and Friday: Thanksgiving, US markets are closed on Thursday, early close at 1:00 p.m. New York time on Friday. Over the long weekend short-dated puts lose value on their own. The Thanksgiving week has been positive for the Nasdaq 100 in 27 of the last 40 years, but not in 2018, when it lost 5.0%.

  • Into month end: pension funds rebalancing toward stocks after the fall.

For the euro, S&P's scheduled review of France comes on Friday and Spain's snap election on Sunday. Then euro area inflation on December 1, payrolls on December 4, the Fed on December 9, US CPI on December 10, the ECB and France's budget deadline on December 17, the Bank of Japan on December 18.

How would I use a rebound?

I would not chase the fall from here. I would use the rebounds. A vanna rally that stalls at 26,450, or in the 27,000 to 27,600 zone, is where I would sell the Nasdaq 100 again and buy put spreads (buying a put and selling a lower one to cap the cost). After such a rally implied volatility is lower, so protection costs less, and the index sits under resistance. That is what the history above favors. A bounce is not a reclaim: what would prove me wrong is a close above 26,450 that holds for several sessions, with a Fed that signals a pause in December.

What comes next for me. This week fits the sequence I have followed since September: the AI shock, then credit, then dollar funding. The first two are in the prices. The third is building outside the United States. That systemic phase is the next chapter I will write.

data.title: Week Ahead: Will The Dollar's Resilience In The Face Of Falling Stocks And Rates Be Challenged?
data.description:
The S&P 500 fell by about 8% last week. It is off almost 9% since the end of September. The Nasdaq Composite fell 10% last week, the sixth weekly decline in the past six weeks. It has fallen by around 16.5% this quarter. Oil prices have also fallen. January WTI fell by about 5%, its third weekly decline. It has fallen by about $20 a barrel since the end of October. 

As one would expect, interest rates have fallen. The US two-year yield fell 23 bp last week and is now off 28 bp since the end of September. The US 10-year yield fell 22 bp last week and it has shed around 37 bp since the end of September. The greenback is more resilient than we expected under these conditions. The US dollar rose to new highs for the year against four of the G10 currencies before the weekend (GBP, AUD, NZD, SEK). Earlier last week, the dollar set the year's high against four other currencies (Euro, CAD, CHF, DKK). That left the yen and Norwegian krone as exceptions. In the risk-off climate, for the most part, the high yielding emerging market currencies underperformed. As we discuss below, while the dollar is looking stretched, encouragement to pick a top is not being provided by the technical evidence. 

U.S.

Drivers: The dollar has fared better than we expected given the pullback in US equities and the wavering of the AI meme. The drag has been offset, it appears, by the stronger than expected October job gains and the hotter than expected inflation that pushed up short-term US rates. However, late last week, the drop in oil prices and equities dragged rates lower but the greenback remained resilient. The rolling 30-day correlation of changes in the Dollar Index and the two-year US yield has risen from below 0.20 as recently as November 9 to a little more than 0.50, the most since early October. From late March through late October the correlation of changes in the US two-year yield and the S&P 500 was inverse, but now it is positively correlated, slightly less than 0.45. The high for the year was recorded in March around 0.60. 

Data: Outside of the Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday, the US economic diary is full this coming week. The highlights include the preliminary November PMI on Monday, and October personal income, consumption, and deflators, alongside revisions to Q3 GDP, and the Fed's Beige Book on Wednesday, and the preliminary estimate of the October goods balance on Black Friday. Yet, given the solid jobs report, the acceleration of CPI and PPI, and hawkish comments by several Fed officials, the market is already fully discounting a hike at next month's FOMC meeting. Indeed, partly given Governor Waller's suggestion, the Fed funds futures are pricing in almost a 10% chance of a 50 bp move. The market is discounting 78 bp of tightening between now and the end of H1 27, up from 38 bp before the October jobs report. 

Prices: The Dollar Index approached 104.00 last week, its best level since "Liberation Day" in April 2025. The 104.60 area corresponds to the (61.8%) retracement of DXY's decline that began a few days before President Trump's second inauguration in January 2025. Momentum indicators are stretched but do not look poised to turn lower. Still, expectations for the trajectory of Fed policy have become somewhat more restrained given the drop in oil and equity prices. 

EMU

Drivers: Over the past 30 sessions, changes in the euro are more inversely correlated with changes in the US 10-year yield (~-0.44) than changes in the US two-year yield (~-0.40). The euro is more (inversely) correlated with US rates than German rates. The euro's inverse correlation with changes in Germany's two-year yield is around -0.26 and the with the 10-year Bund yield about -0.33. The 30-day correlation with changes in the two-year interest rate differential is almost -0.23, while the correlation with changes in the 10-year differential is about -0.32. Meanwhile, the French mini-crisis has passed, at least for the moment, and this has seen the euro's correlation with the German discount to France fall back to almost 0.25 from around 0.60 in mid-October. 

Data: The eurozone sees its flash November PMI at the start of the week and the ECB's inflation survey at the end of the week. The data is unlikely to have much impact. After expanding by 0.4% in Q3, the median forecast in Bloomberg's survey is for 0.3% growth over the next few quarters. The swaps market continues to discount a strong probability of a rate hike next month (~90%). It has about 58 bp of tightening discounted between now and the end of H1 27. The French premium over Germany has not been less than 140 bp in a month. It was less than 80 bp until late June. By late September it was pushing beyond 100 bp and reached 174 bp in October. It is now near 155 bp. 

Prices: The euro continues to struggle to sustain even the most modest of upticks. However, the downside momentum seemed to stall last week after the euro approached $1.0950 in the middle of the week. It did not settle above $1.10 last week. The $1.0880 area corresponds to the (61.8%) retracement of the euro's rally from the early 2025 low (~ $1.0140). The euro has not settled above the previous session high since November 4. We are looking some technical indication of a bottom and a close above $1.10 would be a step in the right direction. 

PRC

Drivers: The PBOC continues to guide the exchange rate. We continue to watch the dollar's daily fix for clues of the official intent. There does not appear to have been a change since reserve requirements on foreign currency deposits were raised earlier this month. 

Data: China reports October industrial profits at the end of the week. On a year-over-year, year-to-date basis, industrial profits rose 15.5% in September. It was the fourth consecutive month of slowing, from the 18.8% in May, which was the strongest since 2021. Mining (drilling) and electronics are strong sectors that offset broader weaknesses. 

Prices: We have suggested that the signal from Chinese officials for a steadier yuan would leave the greenback in a CNH6.65-CNH6.70 range. The upper end was tested on November 19 and it held. This still seems like a reasonable guesstimate. By hugging the dollar, while the dollar has risen against the G10 currencies this month, the yuan is appreciating more broadly than the exchange rate with the dollar may suggest. So far this month, the yuan has risen by more than 2% against half the G10 currencies. It also has appreciated against most emerging market currencies, including more than 8% against the Brazilian real, which will contribute to making Brazil's soy more price attractive. 

Japan

Drivers: The dollar-yen exchange rate has become more correlated with changes in US interest rates, while at the same time, Japanese verbal intervention may be temping enthusiasm near JPY160. The rolling 30-day correlation of changes in the exchange rate and the US two-year yield is slightly below 0.80, and the correlation with changes in the US 10-year yield is around 0.76. Both are the most robust since September 2025. The correlation of changes in the exchange rate and Japan's two-year yield has been inverse since mid-September but popped up to finish the week positive (~0.02). It does not suggest that BOJ expectations are an important consideration now that the market has discounted a strong chance of a hike next month. 

Data: The PMI rarely appears to have impact on Japanese markets or the yen. On the other hand, reports on prices may have more impact. In the middle of the week, October producer services prices are due, but the highlight is Tokyo's November CPI at the end of the week. Tokyo's CPI provides useful insight into price pressures on the national level. The swaps market shows about an 80% chance of a rate hike next month. A little more than another hike is largely discounted in H1 27. 

Prices: Falling US rates saw the greenback fall to JPY158.55 ahead of the weekend, its lowest level since November 10. The next area of support is around JPY158, and a break could target JPY157.40 next. The rejection of the JPY160 area and the losses ahead of the weekend is seeing the daily momentum indicators turn lower. 

UK

Drivers: Sterling has been trending higher against the euro all year and its cross gains. However, in the middle of last week, the euro staged a key upside reversal, and it finished last week with a new high for the month. Ironically, however, changes in sterling are inversely correlated with changes in the UK's two-year yield (-0.45). It reached a little beyond -0.50 in the middle of the month, the most in five months. The inverse correlation between the exchange rate and the US two-year yield is slightly less inverse (~-0.44). Sterling's 30-day correlation with changes in the FTSE 100 rose above 0.50 earlier this month to challenge the year's high seen in May but now has eased to around 0.30.

Data: The UK economy grew 0.7% in Q3 quarter-over-quarter, matching its strongest quarterly performance since Q1 22. The economic highlight this week is the preliminary November PMI. In October, the composite was 52.9, that is the best level since the US/Israel war on Iran began at the end of February. The UK composite PMI rose for the third time in four months. The swaps market is discounting almost a 75% chance of a Bank of England hike next month. Three hikes are nearly fully priced into the market by the middle of next year. 

Prices: Sterling stabilized after falling a new low for the year ahead of the weekend (~$1.3080). The momentum indicators are still falling, even if over-extended and the tone remains fragile. It has fallen for three consecutive weeks. The next important chart area is around $1.2980-$1.3000. A move above $1.3150 would be the first preliminary sign of a bottoming process. 

Canada

Drivers: The US dollar's exchange rate against the Canadian dollar is equally correlated with changes in the US two-year premium over the past 30 sessions and changes in the US two-year yield (~0.45) or the Canadian two-year yield (~0.08, note that the sign is positive). Higher two-year Canadian dollar yields have insignificant but positive correlation with a weaker Canadian dollar. On the other hand, the 30-day correlation of changes in the US 10-year yield and the exchange rate (~0.44) is a little higher than the correlation with the 10-year interest rate differential (~0.37) and changes in Canada's 10-year yield (~0.20). Yet changes in the exchange rate are mostly correlated with changes in the US dollar more broadly. The rolling 30-day correlation between the exchange rate and the Dollar Index is a little above 0.80. It has not been much above 0.85 for around 2 1/2 years. 

Data: Canada reports the results of its October establishment labor market survey November 26. Recall that the October household survey showed a loss of 4.7k jobs and a rise in the unemployment rate to 6.7% (from 6.5%), even though the participation rate was steady. The following day, Canada will report Q3 current account. In Q2, it reported its first quarterly surplus since Q2 22. The market seems to underappreciate the improvement in Canada's external account this year. The merchandise trade balance swung to a C$15.1 bln surplus in the first nine months of the year compared with a deficit of C$27.2 bln in the Jan-Sept 2025 period. Moreover, net portfolio investment inflows more than tripled to C$161.6 bln in the first eight months of 2026 compared with C$50 bln in the same year ago period. 

Prices: The US dollar rose slightly above CAD1.4355 last week, its highest level of the year. Previous resistance around CAD1.4300 now becomes support. Momentum indicators are extended and are looking toppish but that does not mean that a high for the greenback is in place. The greenback has risen for three consecutive weeks after having fallen for the previous three weeks (and rose the five weeks before that. The near-term upside risk may extend into the CAD1.4400-15 area. 

Australia

Drivers: The Australian dollar stands out in that its 30-day correlation with changes in the US two-year yield (less than 0.1) is miniscule while its correlation with changes in Australia's two-year yield (~0.42) is near the most robust in the last couple of years. The most aggressive G10 central bank this year is seen as the most likely candidate to begin easing policy next year. The disappointing employment report saw Australia's two-year yield fall 20 bp last week, the biggest weekly decline in nearly four months. The Australian dollar was the worst performer in the G10 last week, losing a little more than 2%. 

Data:  Four rate hikes by the Reserve Bank of Australia this year appear to be taking an economic toll, but not yet curbing price pressures. The October PMIs were below the 50 boom/bust level. The composite PMI has fallen for three months through October. The preliminary November survey results will be announced Monday. The October CPI will be reported on Wednesday. The September CPI was 4.3%, the highest since March and the base effect (zero in October 2025) underscores the risk of another increase. The trimmed mean CPI was at 3.6%, and here the base effect (0.3% in October 2025) suggests a relatively stable pace. The futures market has grown more confident that the monetary tightening cycle is over and now sees the first cut likely being delivered around mid-2027 is beginning to discount the risk of a cut. 

Prices: The Australian dollar continues to trade poorly. It settled near its lows for the year recorded ahead of the weekend slightly below $0.6610. It has not traded above the previous day's high since November 6, when the US jobs growth surprised to the upside. The Aussie has been punished this month, and its 5.9% decline has stretched momentum indicators, as one would expect, though it has settled above the lower Bollinger Band for the past four sessions. Still, there is no technical sign that a low is in place. The next objective may be around $0.6600, which is the halfway point of the Australian dollar's rally from April 2025 low ($0.5915). Below there lies congestion built in May-November 2025 that extends toward almost $0.6400. 

Mexico 

Drivers:  For the first time since March, changes in the dollar-peso exchange rate and the US two-year yield are inverse over the past 30-sessions (~-0.02). Here, too, it is about the sign more than the magnitude. Nor has the exchange rate been correlated with changes in the Dollar Index. It recorded a low for the year, less than 0.02 last week, down from 0.60 in early October. Even its role as a proxy for emerging market currencies more broadly has waned. The correlation of the exchange rate and changes in the JP Morgan Emerging Market Currency Index was around -0.85 at the end of Q3 and about -0.45 early last week, the least robust in ten months. 

Data: Mexico will take another look at Q3 GDP on Tuesday. Its first estimate was 0.9%, which brought the four-quarter moving-average to 0.73%, the highest since Q3 23. Still, the central bank cut its target rate to 6.25% earlier this month in a 3-2 vote that was characterized as one-off. The CPI for the first half of November is due the next day. At the end of October, the headline and core rates were barely inside the 2%-4% target at 3.88% and 3.82%, respectively. Mexico reports Q3 current account on Wednesday followed by the October trade figures at the end of the week. While Mexico has seen its external balance improve this year, it stalled in Q3. Through September, Mexico reported an average monthly trade surplus of about $1.03 bln compared with an average monthly shortfall of $377.6 mln in the first nine months of 2025. However, in Q3, the trade balance flipped back to an average monthly deficit of $282.8 mln compared with an average monthly surplus of almost $3.6 bln in Q2. Through September, Mexico's exports are up by slightly more than 30% this year. The deterioration of the trade balance warns that Q3 current account balance may have narrowed from $8.9 bln in Q2, which was the largest surplus since Q4 24. On November 27, Banxico issues its quarterly report which it has used in the past to update its macroeconomic forecasts. The swaps market is discounting a hike in late Q2 27. 

Prices: The Mexican peso snapped a two-week rally with prejudice last week. It was thumped for 2.7%. It seems counter-intuitive, but before the two-week rally that ended with the stronger than expected US jobs growth reported on November 6, the Mexican peso fell for the previous eight weeks. The peso's losses were concentrated on November 18-19 when it fell by about 3.6%. With a few exceptions, like the Turkish lira, high yielding emerging market currencies were the hardest hit last week. Latam currencies were three of the five worst performing emerging market currencies (joined the South African rand and Hungarian forint). The US dollar gains last week met the (50%) retracement objective of its slide from the early 2025 high near MXN21.29. That retracement was MXN19.0750. It moved above it in the past two sessions but was unable to close above it. Although it has been a big move, the momentum indicators and price action warns the upside may not have been exhausted. The next retracement (61.8%) is near MXN19.60.

data.title: MLPs Explained: Not All Dividends Are Created Equal
data.description:
At The Oxford Club, we often say, “It’s not how much you make; it’s how much you keep.”

Which would you rather do: make $10,000, pay 24% in taxes for a net of $7,600, and continue to pay tax on any money it earns… or make $8,000 tax-deferred, allowing it to grow for years without paying any taxes?

The obvious answer is to make a lower gross but higher net.

What if, instead of a lower gross, you could earn a substantially higher amount… like $83,800 instead of $10,000?

The current dividend yield of the S&P 500 is a hair over 1%.

Yet there is a class of stocks with an average yield of 8.38% where most − and sometimes all − of the dividend is tax-deferred. Instead of earning $10,000 in dividends from the S&P 500, you could earn eight times that amount in this special group.

I’m talking about master limited partnerships (MLPs).

Many MLPs are in the energy sector, which means they are likely to participate in the AI boom, as oil- and gas-thirsty data centers and utilities need massive amounts of energy to fuel the rise in AI.

By the same token, regardless of AI, homes and businesses need more energy as well. It’s hard to imagine a meaningful decline in energy demand.

There are non-energy MLPs too.

AllianceBernstein Holding (NYSE: AB), a stock that’s currently in my Oxford Income Letter portfolio, is an asset manager with a big 11% yield. New England Realty Associates LP (NYSE: NEN) owns and operates apartments, condos, and commercial properties.

When you own an MLP, you are a partner, not a shareholder, and you receive distributions, not dividends. For most MLPs, the majority of the distribution − if not all of it − is considered a return of capital, which is not taxable. Instead, it lowers your cost basis.

It works like this.

Let’s say you bought an MLP for $20 a share. In Year 1, you receive $1 in distributions. Your new cost basis is $19, because your original $20 cost basis is reduced by the $1 distribution.

You receive $1 per share in each of the next four years. Your cost basis is now $15.

Over those five years, you did not owe any tax on the $5 per share in distributions you received.

After the fifth year, you go to sell the stock when it’s trading at $25. Since your cost basis is now $15, you will owe tax on $10 per share of capital gains instead of $5.

If you own the stock for a long time, as long as your cost basis doesn’t fall to zero, you don’t pay any tax on any of those distributions in any of those years.

MLPs can be an excellent estate planning tool as well. If you pass away, your heirs inherit the stock at a stepped-up cost basis, which means they’ll never have to pay tax on the portions of your distributions that were tax-deferred.

For example, suppose someone buys a stock at $20 and is paid $1 per share in distributions each year for 18 years. They’ve haven’t paid any tax on the $18 worth of distributions.

After 18 years, they pass away. The stock is trading at $40.

Their heirs inherit the stock, and the meter starts running from that new $40 cost basis instead of the original $20 price.

Imagine earning an average of 8% or more per year and collecting the cash − or, even better, reinvesting it to let it compound − without paying tax on it for years.

The tax-deferred feature and high yields are an investor’s dream combination. They’re why MLPs are one of my favorite types of investments.

data.title: When Stocks Crash, Bonds Still Matter
data.description:
Bonds have historically provided a degree of protection during stock market downturns, highlighting their diversification benefits and relatively low correlation with equities. This unusual performance reflected the aggressive interest rate hikes that year, as the Federal Reserve battled elevated inflation, putting pressure on both equity and fixed-income markets. Despite this episode, investors should not overlook the historical role bonds can play as a portfolio hedge during periods of equity market stress.

Notes from this week’s charts:

  • The S&P500 has broken its 200dma and a key support level.

  • In historical context, the current drawdown is not out of the ordinary.

  • Further downside risk stems from allocations, valuations, and wealth effects.

  • Warsh’s will to press on with rate hikes will be tested by market volatility.

  • Euphoric investor sentiment levels have been suddenly slashed.

1. Technically Bearish: this chart is worth pondering for a couple of reasons… First, the index has broken its 200-day moving average, which is an (imperfect) yardstick for uptrend vs downtrend distinction [n.b. over the 10-year period below it correctly flagged the single trend transition during that period (2022), but also gave about a half-dozen false alarms].

The index also previously put in a bearish breadth divergence, and on Friday made an initial breakdown through 7000 (albeit it could easily find support in the zone just below). Overall: bearish looking stuff.

The bullish take would be that it ends up like the other half-dozen episodes where a breach of the 200dma foreshadowed a capitulation, washout, and rebound.

Source: MarketCharts charting tools

2. All Gone Upside Down: looking at it from the inverted side, it looks quite bullish (rounding bottom, breakout vs resistance, breakout through 200dma).

[as a fun game, cover the title and see what your colleagues think]

Source: Topdown Charts Professional

3. Into Context: obligatory context chart; at about -12% the top-to-bottom drawdown this episode is not particularly out of the ordinary when looked at in the context of historical drawdowns.

BUT: one thing sticks out…

(you can count the number of times it went down this much without going further on one finger)

4. More Context: and the risk case is that this unwinds.

Source: Topdown Charts Pro

5. Even More Context — Wealth Effects: there’s another problem on display in this chart. As allocations to equities are so high and because we are coming from such a high starting point valuation(/expectations), if stocks fall big there will be a negative wealth effect; and that will damage the outlook for earnings, which will make stocks fall, and so-on.

It’s a feedback loop. And it’s been helpful in recent years on the way up.

Source: UBS via Daily Chartbook

6. Euphoria Descent: on the pragmatic side, if we’re to look for buying opportunities and rebound odds, here’s one development. The Euphoriameter (combined sentiment gauge) has dropped down to about neutral.

Notably though it did go a little lower in 2018 (which saw similar price action [ranging and then weakness into Q4], and similar issues with overhyped sentiment and Fed rate hikes putting pressure on the market).

7. Fed Put? Warsh’s willingness to focus on economics vs markets will be put to the test in the coming weeks. Yellen yielded after the 2015 hike rattled global markets, and then Powell pivoted after his inherited hiking cycle culminated in the 2018 correction.

Will Warsh wait for markets to find their feet?

8. Global Policy Path: globally the tides have already been turning for some time, and 2026 has seen a big pivot from rate cuts to rate hikes.

Source: Topdown Charts Pro

9. The Bear Market in Bull Markets: as such, it’s not too surprising to see a bear market in bull markets (where bull market is defined as 20% up), and generally bearish price action in global equities.

10. Something on Semis: one optimistic scenario would be that on the topic of analogs, we’re back in 1998 —where there was a major countertrend move, a late-cycle reset; a mini-bear market [albeit you could probably draw more parallels between that period and 2022].

This would be nice, but also, if we took this literally —we’d still have a way to go. SMH is only down -40% across 5-months, the below was -53% across 14-months (so if it played out exactly, you would expect some big rebound rallies, but also further grind lower for at least a few more months before a turnaround like that seen in the chart).

data.title: Commoditization Of Cutting Edge: From Railroads To AI
data.description:
Market prices are as of the 20 November 2026 close unless stated otherwise.

On Friday, Nvidia (NVDA) closed at $125.53. That's below the $142.62 it closed at on 24 January 2025, the session before DeepSeek's cheap model knocked 17% off the stock in a single day. Nearly two years of AI enthusiasm later, the market's favorite AI supplier trades below where it stood before the first scare.

Part of that is Nvidia's own trouble. Jensen Huang resigned on 12 November, and on Friday Reuters reported that SEC enforcement staff are examining potential accounting issues at the company. The slide started before either story, though, and it isn't only Nvidia. The PHLX Semiconductor Index (SOX) closed at 8,408.59, about 43% below its 22 June record close of 14,634.72, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.3% on the day.

One number keeps popping up. US investment in information-processing equipment and software reached 5.35% of GDP in the third quarter of 2026. The dot-com peak was 4.46%, in the fourth quarter of 2000.

US private investment in information-processing equipment and software as a share of nominal GDP, 1947 to Q3 2026. Shading marks NBER recessions. The BEA category covers all IT spending, not only AI.

Source: US BEA via FRED; author's ratio; MoneyTurkey chart.

MoneyTurkey's longer study goes back through seven earlier technology booms to see what followed spending peaks like this one. Here are the parts that matter most for AI.

The Railways Won. Many Backers Didn't.

In 1847 Britain put roughly 7% of its GDP into railways, and the men building the lines numbered about twice the British Army. The railways became the backbone of the economy. The boom still ended in a bust.

America repeated it on a bigger scale. In 1893 alone, more than 27,000 miles of US railroad went into receivership. Yet in 1900 railroads still made up 63% of US stock-market value.

A technology can change the world and still be a poor investment for the people who paid for the build-out. Easy to say. Much harder to act on mid-boom.

Fiber Is The Closer Match

The late-1990s telecom build-out is the most uncomfortable parallel. In the five years after the Telecommunications Act of 1996, carriers put more than $500 billion into fiber, switches and wireless networks. No more than 2% of North American long-distance capacity was in use. Shareholders lost roughly $2 trillion, and about half a million telecom workers lost their jobs.

The product didn't fail. It got cheap. IP transit fell from $1,200 per Mbps a month in 1998 to $0.63 in 2015. Users won outright. The Nasdaq Telecommunications Index fell 92% from February 2000 to September 2002 and is still less than half its 2000 peak. US operating-company IPOs went from 476 in 1999 to 66 in 2002.

The Same Shape, Again And Again

The other cycles rhyme. America had 272 car makers in 1909 and nine by 1941. US airlines filed for bankruptcy 198 times between 1979 and 2016, by their industry body's unofficial count, while real domestic fares fell by nearly half. McKinsey concluded that memory-chip makers "were not able to create economic value between 1996 and 2012." Nokia (NOK) had 49.4% of world smartphone sales in 2007, and six years later Microsoft bought its phone business.

The likelier reading, and it is a judgment rather than a law: the damage for investors tended to come after the peak in capital spending, not the peak in the technology. In MoneyTurkey's study of these cycles, the sector indexes and fallen leaders dropped between 70% and 98% from peak to trough, and several never regained their highs.

Where AI Sits Now

Prices are already collapsing. OpenAI launched GPT-4 in March 2023 at $30 per million input tokens. GPT-5, a far more capable model, launched in August 2025 at $1.25. Epoch AI estimates that the cost of reaching a fixed level of model performance has been falling between 9 and 900 times a year, depending on the benchmark.

For now the supplier still keeps the margin. On 17 November Nvidia reported record quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion, $107.6 billion of it from data centers, at a 74.8% GAAP gross margin. The stock fell anyway.

The buyers are stretching to pay for it. Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT) and Meta Platforms (META) guided to roughly $720 billion to $740 billion of combined 2026 capital spending after their October results, and Fortune reports that four of the five biggest AI spenders had negative free cash flow in the third quarter. Alphabet alone reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion for the quarter. Some of the money is now borrowed or raised. Microsoft priced $25 billion of senior notes on 29 October, and Meta launched $37.5 billion of underwritten stock offerings on 26 October.

The shakeout has started quietly. Big platforms have absorbed start-ups through license-and-hire deals rather than letting them fail: Microsoft with Inflection, Google with Character.AI and Windsurf, Meta with its 49% stake in Scale AI. Seed rounds fell 27% year on year in the third quarter.

The Index Problem

Each era's new technology ended up dominating its home market. Railroads were 63% of US stock-market value in 1900. Information technology was about 33% of the S&P 500 in March 2000. The Magnificent Seven made up 34.9% of the S&P 500 at the end of 2025, and CME Group puts information technology at roughly 39% in mid-2026.

Peak weights of each era's leading technology in its home market index, compared with US railroads in 2017.

Source: UBS/Credit Suisse Global Investment Returns Yearbooks; CME Group; S&P Dow Jones Indices; MoneyTurkey chart.

Each earlier time, that weight later came down. A cap-weighted index fund holds that concentration by design.

What Could Be Different

AI doesn't have to follow the script exactly. Railways and telecom were built largely by leveraged newcomers. Today's biggest spenders are some of the most profitable companies in history and still fund most of their capex from operating cash flow, though that cushion is thinning. That could make any shakeout slower and shallower at the top of the index, and harsher among debt-funded neoclouds and single-product start-ups. Gartner (IT), for one, forecasts that 80% of neocloud companies will have been absorbed or will have shut down by 2030. That's a forecast, not an outcome.

What’s to Watch

A 43% fall in the chip index is a deep correction. It isn't 2000 to 2002 yet, when the SOX fell 80% and took 17.6 years to regain its peak.

The indicator most worth watching is the dull one: IT investment as a share of GDP in the BEA's quarterly figures. In 2000 that line turned before most people called it a bust. If it rolls over while hyperscalers keep borrowing to fund capex, the history above starts to look a lot less academic.

Railways and fiber both got built, and both became cheap for the people who used them. AI is clearly working. What nobody knows yet is who gets to keep the money.

A longer version of this analysis, with all seven cycles and the full data, first appeared on MoneyTurkey.com.

data.title: Disney Produces Mediocre FCF Growth - How To Play DIS After Its Recent Rise
data.description:
The Walt Disney Company (DIS) generated 89% higher FCF in fiscal Q4, ending Oct. 3, but only 4.9% higher for the year. Moreover, in the Nov. 17, 2026, shareholder letter, management guided FCF up just 4% for next year. So, is DIS stock at a peak?

DIS closed down about 1.7% on Friday at $118.11, after rising to a 6-month peak after its results release. Moreover, since its recent low of $101.33 on Oct. 1, DIS stock is up 17.0%.

DIS stock - last 6 months - Barchart - Nov. 20, 2026

Mediocre FCF Growth

FCF for FY 2026 came in at $10.572 billion, just 4.9% higher than the $10.077 billion, as seen on page 11 of its shareholder letter. Moreover, its annual FCF margin fell from 10.67% of revenue last year to 10.33% this year, according to Stock Analysis.

So, since analysts project 4.0% higher revenue in 2027 at $106.52 billion next year, and management is forecasting just $11.0 billion in FCF (i.e., up 4.05%), the FCF margin should stay level at 10.33% next year.

The problem is this mediocre growth rate is already discounted in the stock price after its recent rise. Moreover, analysts and the market want to see better than mediocre FCF growth and higher FCF margins.

DIS Price Targets

Nevertheless, analysts still see DIS stock as undervalued. For example, 32 analysts surveyed by Yahoo! Finance have an average price target (PT) of $131.34. That's about 10.7% higher.

Barchart's mean survey PT is slightly higher at $132.22, and AnaChart's survey of 20 analysts has an average of $132.31. AnaChart's average PT tends to be based on more recent analysts' write-ups. These last 2 PTs are 11.4% higher than its close on Friday.

So, if FCF will only be 5% higher, as management projects, why do these analysts still think there is 10-11% upside left in the stock?

One reason could be that DIS is trading well below its historical average price/earnings (P/E) metric.

For example, Seeking Alpha shows that DIS's forward P/E for the past 5 years has been 21.69x. Analysts' Sept. 2027 $7.57 EPS forecast average puts DIS on a forward P/E of just $15.67x. That implies a 38.4% upside potential (21.69/15.67x-1).

Similarly, Morningstar's 18.9x 5-year historical forward P/E average implies 20.6% upside. The average of these two implies upside of  29.5%.

However, the 5% FCF growth rate provided by management dampens this potential upside. The average of 29.5% and 5.0% is 17.25% upside.

Given a 5% discount rate for one year, the potential upside is just 16.42%, or a PT of $137.34. That is close to where the average of these analysts' price targets are today.

How to Play DIS

Since there may be limited upside, it could make sense for conservative investors to wait for DIS stock to move back down. 

Then the investor can do short-put plays at out-of-the-money (OTM) strike prices, or covered calls if the investor is already a shareholder. Less risk-averse investors can also do short put credit spreads. 

In addition, at that point, some investors might be willing to invest in long-dated in-the-money (ITM) DIS call options.

As a result, some investors may feel it makes sense to wait until there is at least a mid-20% upside potential using several metrics.

data.title: Bitcoin Below $58K As Stablecoin Supply Shrinks $14-17B In A Month
data.description:
Bitcoin (BTC.X) fell below $58,000 on 20 November 2026 after sweeping through the $59,000 to $62,000 liquidation cluster that had sat on the market since August, and the squeeze came as the industry’s own liquidity was draining: stablecoin supply contracted by $14 billion to $17 billion in the 30 days before the break, per Glassnode’s data.

Both liquidity rails dried up at once

The stablecoin contraction matters because stablecoins are the funding side of the futures market. While their supply shrank through November, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded combined net outflows of more than $1.1 billion over the Tuesday-to-Thursday sessions, by Farside Investors data. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) alone lost $541.1 million on Thursday, 19 November, its largest single-day outflow since launch, inside a $582.3 million day for the ETF complex as a whole, even as Q3 13F filings showed endowments holding their IBIT stakes. The 19 November record topped the previous daily outflow high, which Farside data dates to January. Price and flows moved together. CoinGecko data put the low at $57,700 on 20 November, the first break below $60,000 since June, with other tracking showing the session closing near $58,300 to $59,500. Bitcoin had traded above $86,000 in September before a three-month pattern of lower highs and lower lows. Banks had been adding to ETF positions through the third quarter, so the November withdrawal wave marked a sharp turn in institutional behaviour.

What the desks are watching

Glassnode’s 17 November weekly report, ‘Capitulation Meets Support’, flagged the $59,000 to $62,000 zone as the largest liquidation cluster on its six-month futures heatmap, tracing it mostly to leveraged longs opened in August 2026. On 21 November, the firm confirmed the cluster had been fully cleared the day before. It also identified the largest bids since August at $60,000 and below, and warned that a daily close beneath a $62,000 to $66,000 band of recently acquired coins could open a decline toward $53,700. QCP Capital framed the wider conditions: “A meaningful recovery likely needs tech equities to stabilise, rates volatility to fall and institutional flows to return.” A U.S. tech stock index fell to its lowest level since April amid the broader selloff, the backdrop QCP pointed to for why short-covering rallies may struggle until those conditions change. Sentiment echoed the flush. Santiment measured Bitcoin’s bullish-to-bearish social media comment ratio at 0.59 on 20 November, an ‘Extreme Fear’ reading continuing a collapse in crowd confidence that began around mid-September. For traders sizing risk into the next session, the levels in play are $60,000 and below, where Glassnode sees the heaviest bids, and the $53,700 downside trigger.

data.title: Gold Mid-Tiers’ Q3’26 Fundamentals
data.description:
Smaller mid-tier and junior gold miners just finished reporting another great quarter, earning some of their fattest profits ever.  That was no mean feat, as smaller gold miners had to overcome Q3’s big gold swings and surging mining costs.  Like usual mid-tiers well-outperformed the majors.  Yet smaller gold stocks are now trading at record-low valuations, hammered by gold’s recent Fed-rate-hike-fear-driven breakdowns.

The leading mid-tier-gold-stock benchmark is the GDXJ VanEck Junior Gold Miners ETF.  With $6.6b in net assets midweek, it remains the second-largest gold-stock ETF after its big-brother GDX.  That’s dominated by far-larger major gold miners, though there is much overlap between these ETFs’ holdings.  Still misleadingly named, GDXJ is overwhelmingly a mid-tier gold-stock ETF with juniors having lesser weightings.

Gold-stock tiers are defined by miners’ annual production rates in ounces of gold.  Small juniors have little sub-300k outputs, medium mid-tiers run 300k to 1,000k, large majors yield over 1,000k, and huge super-majors operate at vast scales exceeding 2,000k.  Translated into quarterly terms, these thresholds shake out under 75k, 75k to 250k, 250k+, and 500k+.  Today only six of GDXJ’s 25 biggest holdings are true juniors.

Their Q3 outputs are highlighted in blue in this essay’s table.  Juniors not only mine less than 75k ounces per quarter, but gold output generates over half their quarterly revenues.  That excludes streaming and royalty companies that purchase future gold output for big upfront payments helping finance mine-builds, and primary silver miners producing byproduct gold.  But mid-tiers often make better investments than juniors.

These gold miners dominating GDXJ offer a unique mix of sizable diversified production, excellent output-growth potential, and smaller market capitalizations ideal for outsized gains.  Mid-tiers are less risky than juniors, while amplifying gold uplegs more than majors.  So we’ve long specialized in the fundamentally-superior mid-tiers and juniors at Zeal, actively trading these smaller gold miners for over a quarter-century now.

Technically GDXJ fared well in Q3 proper, rallying 16.0% to amplify gold’s 3.4% gains by 4.8x.  That was strong outperformance, as typically smaller gold miners tend to leverage their metal by 3x to 4x+.  Those quarterly gains didn’t accrue gradually though, as gold saw opposing big swings within Q3.  In mid-July, gold’s necessary and healthy serious reckoning finally bottomed after its late monster record cyclical bull.

Then gold soon blasted higher in a huge August, fueled by a major upside breakout from a massive bullish falling-wedge chart pattern and the US Treasury upping its longer-bond buybacks.  By late August gold had soared 17.4% in under six weeks, which GDXJ amplified 2.8x with a big-and-fast 48.3% rally!  But those promising young uplegs were scuttled in late August by heavy gold selling on Fed-rate-hike fears.

First in late August Trump’s Fed chairman talked a big hawkish game on fighting inflation at this central bank’s annual Jackson Hole symposium.  Then in mid-September this Warsh Fed executed its first hike in 3.1 years at 25 basis points.  Next in early November a Fed governor started pushing for a 50bp hike at the FOMC’s next meeting in early December.  All that spawned gold-futures selling, hitting the metal and miners.

By quarter-end gold and GDXJ had retreated 11.0% and 16.1% from their late-August interim highs, prior to this recent mini-mania in Fed-rate-hike expectations.  At 1.5x downside leverage, smaller gold stocks proved quite resilient.  But more bouts of rate-hike-fear-driven selling in recent weeks slammed gold and GDXJ’s total losses since late August to 20.1% and 33.7% as of midweek, still making for a modest 1.7x.

That vexing 2.8-month-old drubbing has left mid-tier and junior gold stocks deeply out of favor, mired in universal bearishness and apathy.  But the best times to buy relatively low are episodes like these when few others are willing.  The usual post-earnings-season fundamental analyses must go on, despite the lack of interest always accompanying deeply-oversold technicals.  The smaller gold miners continue to thrive.

For 42 quarters in a row now, I’ve painstakingly analyzed the latest operational and financial results from GDXJ’s 25-largest component stocks.  Mostly mid-tiers, they now account for 63.2% of this ETF’s total weighting.  While digging through quarterlies is a ton of work, understanding smaller gold miners’ latest fundamentals really cuts through the obscuring sentiment fogs shrouding this sector.  This research is essential.

This table summarizes the GDXJ top 25’s operational and financial highlights during Q3’26.  These gold miners’ stock symbols aren’t all US listings, and are preceded by their rankings changes within GDXJ over this past year.  The shuffling in their ETF weightings reflects shifting market caps, which reveal both outperformers and underperformers since Q3’25.  Those symbols are followed by their current GDXJ weightings.

Next comes these gold miners’ Q3’26 production in ounces, along with their year-over-year changes from the comparable Q3’25.  Output is the lifeblood of this industry, with investors generally prizing production growth above everything else.  After are the costs of wresting that gold from the bowels of the earth in per-ounce terms, both cash costs and all-in sustaining costs.  The latter help illuminate miners’ profitability.

That’s followed by a bunch of hard accounting data reported to securities regulators, quarterly revenues, earnings, operating cash flows, and resulting cash treasuries.  Blank data fields mean companies hadn’t disclosed that particular data as of the middle of this week.  The annual changes aren’t included if they would be misleading, like comparing negative numbers or data shifting from positive to negative or vice-versa.

Gold miners’ operational performances depend on prevailing gold prices, production growth, and cost control.  Mid-tiers and juniors fared pretty well in Q3 on these fronts, leading to great results.  Yet today’s battered stock prices certainly aren’t reflecting those, with irrational bearish sentiment dragging technicals far under reasonable levels.  This huge technical-fundamental disconnect is a big opportunity for contrarians.

Unlike its big-brother GDX, GDXJ’s top holdings are much more dynamic.  Mid-tiers and juniors with new mines or major expansions going live can fly into its upper ranks on soaring market capitalizations, crowding stagnating ones out.  There’s also big overlap between GDXJ and GDX top holdings.  GDXJ’s 11 largest components are also all GDX-top-25 ones, and the entire GDXJ-top-25 lineup is also included in GDX!

Again accounting for 63.2% of GDXJ’s weighting, they also represent 25.1% of GDX’s.  GDXJ essentially lops off GDX’s 11 largest components which are super-majors and majors, then expands the weighting of the next biggest from a bit over 1/4th to roughly 2/3rds.  Occasionally these dominant gold-stock ETFs’ common manager removes a larger miner from GDXJ to be exclusively included in GDX, like in this past year.

For three quarters in a row into Q4’25, Pan American Silver (PAAS) was GDXJ’s largest holding.  Despite mining 6,070k ounces of silver in Q3’26, PAAS remains a primary gold miner.  Its 168k ounces of gold produced last quarter drove over 7/10ths of its revenues!  PAAS is now GDX’s 10th-largest component.  And PAAS being included in GDXJ-top-25 results in Q3’25 but not Q3’26 definitely skews some year-over-year comparisons.

These elite mid-tiers’ and juniors’ collective gold production weighed in at 2,778k ounces last quarter, sliding 7.8% YoY.  That was better than the GDX top 25’s falling 8.6% YoY to 7,253k, but way behind world gold-mining output.  The World Gold Council publishes gold’s best-available global supply-and-demand data once a quarter in its fantastic Gold Demand Trends reports, which are must-reads for gold-stock traders.

Last quarter’s global gold production grew an impressive 2.9% YoY to 34,430k ounces!  This made for the best Q3 output on record according to the WGC.  It’s unfortunate the GDXJ-top-25 miners didn’t track closer, but this was skewed low.  Excluding PAAS from Q3’25 output while adding in GDXJ’s then-26th-largest component’s improves this to -5.8% YoY.  B2Gold (BTG) also suffered a big 24.1% YoY or 61k-ounce drop.

That was planned, driven by one of its mines finishing its open-pit phase while another largely spent 2026 stripping lower-grade ores.  Primary silver miner Hecla also saw its gold output plummet 70.5% YoY or by 29k ounces.  Earlier this year HL decided to sell its lone primary gold mine to refocus on silver mining.  So elite smaller gold miners’ production decline in Q3 is considerably more modest than the GDXJ top 25’s implies.

Despite GDXJ’s ongoing composition changes led by larger miners periodically graduating into GDX exclusivity, smaller gold miners are still outperforming.  Relative to the GDXJ top 25’s overall production through the last 42 quarters of this research, Q3’s was 35% up in.  That is far better than the GDX top 25’s last quarter just 19% up in.  With a whopping 155 components, GDXJ also has a lower proportion in its upper ranks.

Mid-tiers have always been superior to the majors.  Running smaller stables of typically one-to-four gold mines, any sizable expansions or new mine-builds really move the needle to grow mid-tiers’ production.  They not only usually overcome depletion unlike their larger peers, but often achieve sizable output growth as a group.  Smaller gold stocks enjoy outsized gains around new expansions and mines coming online.

Production growth is essential in gold mining because it provides the cashflows necessary to continue expanding existing mines and building or buying new ones, ultimately driving stock prices higher.  And surprisingly mid-tiers often have lower mining costs than majors, despite the latter’s supposed economies of scale.  That makes mid-tiers much more profitable relative to their production, supporting bigger stock gains.

Also contributing to those is mid-tiers’ lower market capitalizations.  The GDXJ top 25’s averaged merely $8.6b this week, around 1/4th of the GDX top 25’s $33.0b average last week!  Generally the smaller any company’s market cap, the less inertia its stock price has and the less capital inflows needed to drive it higher.  So when gold is powering higher fueling sector interest, mid-tiers and juniors really outperform.

As usual in this long research thread, immediately after earnings season I started with the GDX top 25’s Q3’26 results which I analyzed in depth in last week’s essay.  Comparing the mid-tier-dominated GDXJ’s quarterlies with the major-dominated GDX’s helps explain smaller gold miners’ outperformance which is also evident in stock prices.  GDXJ again tends to amplify major gold moves 3x to 4x+, besting GDX’s 2x to 3x.

Unit gold-mining costs are generally inversely proportional to gold-production levels.  That’s because gold mines’ total operating costs are largely fixed during pre-construction planning stages, when designed throughputs are determined for plants processing gold-bearing ores.  Their nameplate capacities don’t change quarter-to-quarter, requiring similar levels of infrastructure, equipment, and employees to keep running.

So excluding rarer mine expansions, existing mines have fixed tonnages of ores they can process each quarter.  That makes ore grades fed into their plants the primary variable driving gold production, and those vary widely even within individual gold deposits.  Richer ores yield more ounces to spread mining’s big fixed expenses across, lowering unit costs and boosting profitability.  And over time mines’ ore grades decline.

Cash costs are the classic measure of gold-mining costs, including all cash expenses necessary to mine each ounce of gold.  But they are misleading as a true cost measure, excluding the big capital needed to explore for gold deposits and build mines.  So cash costs are best viewed as survivability acid-test levels for smaller gold miners.  They illuminate the minimum gold prices necessary to keep the mines running.

Last quarter the GDXJ top 25’s average cash costs soared 23.9% YoY to a record $1,479 per ounce!  In past years occasional similar cash-cost jumps were seen, but they only lasted one quarter.  2026’s first three have witnessed GDXJ-top-25 cash costs soar 25.9%, 24.8%, and that 23.9% YoY!  The global inflation unleashed by Trump’s war with Iran has driven up global mining costs considerably, led by diesel.

All the heavy equipment necessary to mine gold including giant excavators and massive haul trucks runs on diesel.  Plenty of the GDXJ top 25 mentioned diesel prices as a key driver for their higher mining costs last quarter.  Artemis Gold for example narrowed its 2026 cost guidance to “the very top end” of its range because of “general inflationary pressures, including higher diesel prices”.  Diesel has utterly soared this year.

Even in the US in Q3, national-average retail diesel prices skyrocketed 48.1% YoY to $5.56 per gallon!  And realize the US runs a huge diesel-production surplus and remains the world’s largest exporter of that essential industry fuel.  Many of the world’s gold mines are in remote areas in less-developed countries where sourcing adequate diesel is more expensive and challenging.  Mining is getting costlier globally.

All-in sustaining costs are far superior than cash costs, and were introduced by the World Gold Council in June 2013.  They add on to cash costs everything else that is necessary to maintain and replenish gold-mining operations at current output tempos.  AISCs give a much-better understanding of what it really costs to maintain gold mines as ongoing concerns, and reveal smaller gold miners’ true operating profitability.

The GDXJ top 25’s average AISCs last quarter climbed 11.9% YoY to a record $1,533 per ounce.  Cash costs are the lion’s share of AISCs, so whatever drives the former heavily affects the latter.  Yet despite these rising mining costs, the GDXJ top 25 still trounced the GDX top 25.  The majors dominating GDX saw average AISCs soar 22.0% YoY in Q3 to a far-higher $1,883 per ounce!  But that’s not a clean comparison.

One of the GDXJ-top-25 components in both Q3’26 and Q3’25 was Peru’s Buenaventura, which has long reported the impossible.  Last quarter it declared gold all-in sustaining costs of -$5,029 per ounce!  How is such sorcery even feasible?  BVN is an unusual non-primary-gold miner still choosing to report in gold-centric terms, likely because gold stocks draw much more investor interest and capital than base-metals ones.

In Q3’26 Buenaventura’s gold output accounted for just 29% of its revenues, yet this polymetallic miner still inexplicably chooses to credit its collectively-much-larger silver, copper, zinc, and lead production as gold byproducts gutting its AISCs.  Last quarter one of its mines yielded 13.5k metric tons of copper, 390k ounces of silver, and negligible gold.  Yet that mine still reported ludicrous gold AISCs of -$42,764 per ounce!

Interestingly the jig is finally up on this nonsensical AISC reporting, maybe partially thanks to my years of gold-miner-results essays illuminating it.  Topping BVN’s Q3’26 report’s AISC section, a boldfaced new line was added declaring “Beginning 4Q26, the Company will report All-in Sustaining Cost (AISC) by mine, expressed per unit of each mine’s primary metal”.  That’s the way it always should’ve been done of course.

This implies the years of Buenaventura’s crazy-negative AISCs dragging down the averages are over, which is good news.  But for the entire 42-quarter history of this research thread, I’ve always included all reported data no matter how distorted some was.  Nearly all outlying AISCs have proven anomalous high-side ones, dragging up GDXJ-top-25 averages.  So for consistency’s stake I have to include BVN’s low outliers.

But to illustrate BVN’s distorting skew, excluding its negative AISCs in both Q3’26 and Q3’25 leaves the GDXJ top 25’s average AISCs surging 22.7% YoY to $1,897 per ounce.  Both are right in line with the GDX top 25’s $1,883 up 22.0% YoY.  BVN has also made the GDX-top-25 ranks in past years, but not in either of these relevant quarters.  It ranked as 30th last week, and I sure hope its AISC-skewing days are over.

Rather than worrying about absolute AISC changes, more relevant is their ratio relative to prevailing gold prices.  In Q3’26 the GDXJ top 25’s $1,533 BVN-skewed average merely ran 36.0%, which was the fourth best ever after the preceding three quarters!  For comparison in the five years before Q4’23 birthed that late record gold bull, that AISC-to-gold ratio averaged a far-higher 68%.  Smaller gold miners are doing fine.

After my quarter-century-plus of intensely studying this sector, I’ve found the best metric for measuring gold miners’ collective fundamental performance is their implied unit earnings.  That simply subtracts the GDXJ-top-25 average AISCs from the quarterly-average gold price.  This is way cleaner than bottom-line accounting profits, since a varying GDXJ-top-25 subset’s are usually distorted by big noncash charges or gains.

Gold’s $4,261 average last quarter proved its third-highest ever, surging 23.2% YoY.  That less those GDXJ-top-25 average AISCs of $1,533 yields fat implied sector unit profits of $2,729 per ounce!  Those are the smaller gold miners’ third best ever, and surged an impressive 30.6% YoY despite last quarter’s struggles!  And this wasn’t one-off earnings growth, but the latest in a long parade of quarterly windfall profits.

Astoundingly over the last 13 consecutive quarters ending Q3’26, the GDXJ-top-25 implied unit earnings have skyrocketed 106%, 133%, 63%, 63%, 71%, 95%, 91%, 79%, 82%, 102%, 131%, 68%, and that 31% YoY!  There can’t be any other sector in all the stock markets even remotely competing with such massive consistent profits growth, it is phenomenal.  But this long streak is likely to give up its ghost in Q4.

Because of gold’s irrational Fed-rate-hike-fear-driven breakdowns so far in Q4, it is now averaging $4,049 quarter-to-date.  These are still great gold levels, the fifth-highest quarter ever at this point.  Yet that still would be down 2.5% YoY.  If quarterly-average gold prices indeed finish Q4 slumping, it will be their first negative quarter since Q4’22!  Gold miners will still earn hefty profits, but their earnings-growth streak will end.

That’s not a problem given smaller gold miners’ record-low valuations, so let’s head there through their hard accounting results reported to securities regulators in Q3 under GAAP or other countries’ equivalents.  Even losing PAAS, the GDXJ top 25’s total revenues surged 16.1% YoY to $15,562m which was their third highest ever.  Those fueled bottom-line earnings jumping 20.0% YoY to $3,480m, their fourth highest.

Such strong earnings combined with recently-battered gold-stock prices have pounded the GDXJ-top-25 average trailing-twelve-month price-to-earnings ratios back down to 14.7x!  That’s the lowest they’ve ever been, deeply undervalued.  For reference in Q4’23 when gold’s late monster record bull was born, that ran 45.0x.  Quarterly-average GDXJ levels more than tripled across this span, yet valuations still crashed by 2/3rds!

If you’re contrarian-enough to want to buy fundamentally-superior smaller gold stocks low, they’ve never been cheaper relative to their underlying earnings!  And they are super-oversold too after recent weeks’ pummeling.  Midweek GDXJ closed at just 77.5% of its baseline 200-day moving average, which is the most-oversold smaller gold miners have been in fully 4.0 years!  This sector is a screaming bargain today.

The GDXJ top 25’s operating cash flows climbed 12.0% YoY in Q3 to $5,552m, their fourth highest ever.  That helped catapult their collective cash treasuries up 43.9% YoY to $17,970m, narrowly achieving a new all-time record!  The smaller gold miners have prudently accrued vast cash warchests to fund future production growth, through expanding existing mines and building new ones.  Their fundamentals are great.

We’re constantly looking for the ever-changing highest-production-growth subset of mid-tiers and juniors with big new expansions or mine-builds soon coming online.  Those provide catalysts to attract in capital, particularly from fund managers.  Sooner or later some critical mass of professional investors is going to increasingly recognize the extreme value in this small sector, and flood in catapulting stock prices way higher.

The bottom line is smaller gold miners just reported one of their best quarters ever.  That’s despite surging inflation fueled by Trump’s war catapulting mining costs higher.  Mid-tiers’ and juniors’ remarkable streak of enormous profits growth extended to 13 consecutive quarters, though it will probably end in this current Q4.  Yet even with ongoing cost pressures and gold’s recent breakdowns, gold-mining profits will remain hefty.

Between years of windfall profits and recently-battered stock prices, smaller gold miners’ valuations have fallen to record lows.  Gold stocks have never been cheaper relative to their own underlying corporate earnings.  That combined with extreme oversoldness makes this a great buying opportunity for contrarian speculators and investors.  Gold-stock prices need to mean-revert way higher to reflect their great fundamentals.
