Miami, FL, November 22nd, 2026, FinanceWire


Fresh from its launch in the United Arab Emirates in October, Le Must, the prestige single-serve condiments and preserves brand endorsed by Forbes Travel Guide, today announced its official launch in Europe.

The brand will make its European debut at Les Places d'Or, Hotel & Restaurant, the selective trade show for luxury hotels and fine dining, held November 23, 24 and 25, 2026 in the salons of the Hôtel Le Meurice in Paris. The European business is led by Le Must Europe, based in Paris, with Oshibori Concept as distributor and launch partner.

Le Must built its reputation in the United States, Mexico and the Caribbean, where it is served at Forbes Five-Star hotels and resorts including Four Seasons, The Ritz-Carlton, Mandarin Oriental, Waldorf Astoria and St. Regis, as well as aboard luxury cruise lines and private jets. The brand is endorsed by Forbes Travel Guide through Astria. Europe is the next step in the brand's global expansion.

Le Must's condiments and preserves are made in France, and every product is designed to elevate the guest experience while respecting the planet. The brand is leading the move to plastic-free and biocompostable materials in single-serve packaging, beginning with its biocompostable sugar packets, making it both the ultimate luxury single-serve brand and the most eco-friendly one. American favorites will follow, including the hot sauces and maple syrup that rank among the brand's top sellers. Le Must products were also recently featured in VIP hospitality lounges at select international motorsport events in Europe.

“European hoteliers set the standard for hospitality, and they know a guest remembers the smallest details of a stay,” said Moshe Cohen, President of Le Must Europe. “We are proud to present Le Must at Le Meurice and to offer Europe's finest hotels a collection that is as responsible as it is refined.” Oshibori Concept, the Paris house founded by Franck Salama that creates luxury refreshing towels for prestige hotels and restaurants, will distribute Le Must and lead its promotion across the European market.
“Oshibori Concept was created to give exceptional hotels a gesture of welcome worthy of them, and Le Must brings that same philosophy to the breakfast table,” said Franck Salama, Founder and CEO of Oshibori Concept. “Beauty, quality and responsibility: it is exactly what European hoteliers are looking for.”

Now in its fourth edition, Les Places d'Or, Hotel & Restaurant gathers some fifty high-end brands before a selected audience of hoteliers, restaurateurs, architects, interior designers and investors. The show is open from 4:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m. each day, and industry professionals can request an invitation at visiterhotel.lesplacesdor.com.

About Le Must Europe

Le Must creates prestige single-serve condiments and preserves for the world's finest hotels, resorts, luxury cruise lines and private aviation operators. The brand is endorsed by Forbes Travel Guide through Astria and is committed to plastic-free, biocompostable packaging. Le Must Europe, based in Paris, leads the brand's business in Europe. Learn more at www.lemust.com.

Oshibori Concept is a Paris house that creates luxury refreshing towels for prestige hotels, restaurants and events.

data.title: Crypto Fear And Greed Index Slumps To 7: Can Bitcoin, Ethereum And XRP Rebound?
data.description:
The Crypto Fear and Greed Index has been in a strong sell-off this month as Bitcoin (BTC.X) and most altcoins have continued their plunge. It dropped to the extreme fear zone of 7, down sharply from the year-to-date high of over 72. 

Bitcoin has slumped to $60,000 from the October high of $87,586. Ethereum (ETH-X) has plunged to $1,662, down by over 40% from its highest point in September. XRP (XRP-X) has also fallen by over 60% from its peak in September.

Crypto Fear and Greed Index has plunged

There is a sense that fear is spreading in the market. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index has tumbled to 7. This is important because the index is created by looking at several major data points, including price momentum, volatility, derivative markets, market composition, and proprietary data. 

The same trend is happening with the CNN Money Fear and Greed Index, which has dropped to the extreme fear zone of 10. Most of its gauges, including market momentum, stock price breadth, put and call options, market volatility, safe-haven demand, and junk bond demand, have tumbled to the extreme fear zone. 

These metrics have moved amid major risks in the market. For example, there are signs that the artificial intelligence (AI) bubble is about to burst, which explains why most companies in the industry have plunged. This includes popular names like SanDisk (SNDK), Marvell Technologies (MRVL), and Nvidia (NVDA).

At the same time, there are signs that the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates at its next meeting. Recent data showed that the economy created over 165k jobs last month, while the unemployment rate fell to 4.2%.

Binance hack and ETF outflows

Meanwhile, the Crypto Fear and Greed Index dropped because of the recent Binance hack that cost the company billions of dollars. North Korean hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance. Binance talked to Circle and Tether, which managed to freeze about $3 billion of these funds. The company has also used its funds to top up its reserves. 

Some analysts believe that the Binance hack marked a turning point in the ongoing crypto winter. For one, if Binance, the biggest crypto exchange, can be hacked, then no other company is safe. 

Meanwhile, investors have continued selling their crypto ETFs. Bitcoin ETFs have suffered over $3.5 billion in outflows this month after they shed $550 million last month. Ethereum and XRP ETFs have also shed substantial assets in the past few weeks. In most cases, these outflows tend to signal that investors are starting to capitulate. 

The same trend is happening in the futures market, where open interest has been in a strong sell-off. Falling open interest is a sign that leveraged investors are not buying the coin. One reason for this is that Democrats have retaken the House of Representatives and Senate, opening the door for more regulations.

Technicals are also signaling that cryptocurrencies have more downside to go. Bitcoin and Ethereum have all formed a death cross pattern, pointing to a sustained sell-off. These technicals mean that Bitcoin and altcoins may fall further.

On the positive side, US bond yields are falling, which is a positive thing for risky assets. The drop has coincided with the falling US stock market. As such, with equities plunging, there are signs that the Fed will not hike rates aggressively. In fact, the CME Fed Futures tool shows that the probability is that the bank will hike by 0.25%. Just last week, there was an expectation that the Fed would hike by 0.50%.

data.title: When Sequence Risk Kicks The Door In
data.description:
Markets got crazy this week. What should we do? Buy more? Sell it all? Is it bunker time? Is a recession coming? Is it 2002 all over again? Let’s talk about it.

The wheels started to come off the AI trade this week. It’s an interesting thing to think about because this has to be the most predictable of downturns I can ever remember. I’ve been talking about tech as a very risky and super long duration instrument for years now. In our recent piece on valuations I discussed how investors needed to be careful about tech exposure because the Defined Duration of technology was exposing portfolios to excessive sequence risk. And boy, that sequence risk didn’t just knock on the door this week. It kicked it right down. Figure 1 shows the semiconductor index since the Summer high.

Yes, you read that correctly. That’s a 40% drawdown and the index is still up 12% this year. Amazing stuff. But again, as I’ve said many times in recent years, high valuations are high expectations and when those high expectations disappoint you get big volatility because the margin for error is so slim. It’s interesting in the context of semis because you still have a high annual return, but the sequence risk of the returns just got really messy. So here we are. Expectations are adjusting.

The question now is how much of this is a real economic downturn versus an expectations disappointment because those two things are very different. A revaluation from very high expectations is a good thing in the long-run. That is just a market that recalibrates to a more sustainable baseline. The stock market cannot and should not only go up. It’s a constant give and take across a long-term price discovery path. And that is consistent with your standard correction and short-term bear market which is the market adjusting in the short-term in the process of a longer bull market. A revaluation due to real economic downturn is more troubling because you get a revaluation of prices that is not just psychological price discovery, but a fundamental adjustment to a changing economic regime. Downturns like this become self reinforcing and more sustained because the price discovery process undergoes a much longer and uncertain adjustment as the broader macroeconomy recalibrates. This is where sequence risk shows up and it’s why market downturns like 1929, 1973, 2000 and 2008 lasted as long as they did.

One thing we know about today’s environment is that the downturn is mostly AI driven. We can see this in the dispersion of returns from something like the equal weight index vs the Nasdaq 100. Equal weight is down 7.85% from its peak while the Nas 100 is down 20%. That makes sense because the concern right now is not so much about the broader economy, but AI’s impact more specifically as investors digest how much economic impact will materialize from a reduction of AI investment in the future. The question, as we’ll see here shortly, is whether this spreads like a virus into the broader economy.

Here are my estimates of how this has looked in recent years. As you can see, AI is doing real work in the economy now. Without it we’re growing 1-2%. But the bigger economic worry is the outlier effect of the stock downturn and the wealth effect and then whether the Fed tightens the screws at the same time. A reversal in AI spend doesn’t have the derail the economy, but a negative wealth effect with a tight Fed certainly could.

I’ve put together three general scenarios that could play out from here:

1. AI spending plateaus. The roughly 1 point gross boost goes to zero. Imports fall too, so the net hit is more like 0.3 to 0.7 points. Growth slows to around 1.5% to 2%. That’s painful for tech earnings but not a recession.

2. AI spending gets cut 20% to 30%. The boost turns into a drag, and GDP growth takes a 1 to 1.5 point hit. Growth falls to around 0.5% to 1%. That’s stall speed, and the risk of a recession goes up a lot.

3. The wealth effect adds to either one. Total lost market value is at about $8.5 trillion from the peak. A common rule of thumb is that households cut spending by a few cents for every dollar of stock wealth they lose. If that holds, this hit could cost another 0.5-0.75 points or so of GDP over the next year or two, mostly from upper-income households. This is essentially your 2002 downturn. You don’t necessarily get sustained negative GDP in that environment, but you’ll get enough of a bump in unemployment that the BLS will call it a recession.

There’s an important difference between the Nasdaq Bubble and the current environment though – the companies losing market value aren’t a bunch of profitless dotcom companies with no established business. In this downturn we’re talking about the biggest and most valuable companies that ever existed. They not only have gigantic revenues from AI, but their core businesses are also still very valuable. In 2002 the broader stock market got pulled down because tech fell a whopping 80%. But when we look at the current potential downturn in stocks I think it’s very unlikely that this turns into a 2002 level downturn where the broader market falls 40%+ because the drag from tech is unlikely to rival the same 80% downturn we saw during 2002. That’s a very important difference here.

There’s another very important factor in all of this – that thing called the Federal Reserve. And it adds a 4th scenario in all of this because the response of the Fed in the coming years could be very important.

Here’s the thing about the current state of Fed policy – I don’t think more hikes will hurt the economy much because the Fed basically froze the real estate market with anything over a 6% mortgage. Staying restrictive doesn’t hurt the economy, it just doesn’t help. BUT, rate cuts would have a huge impact here. If the AI slowdown spreads and GDP growth slows to 0% the whole environment starts to look a lot like the 2002 downturn. But one very important difference is if the Fed starts to cut and mortgage rates start to fall materially you’re going to see a big comeback in real estate. Real estate was booming in 2000 and when the Fed cut during the tech bust the impact was minimal. But in 2026 real estate has basically been in its own contained 3 year recession. So you’re going to have a very significant recovery in the economy’s most important sector if the Fed decides it wants that. And that would put a floor under any major market and economic downturn. That’s one of the weird thing about recent growth – AI has been the thing holding up growth during a real estate recession. So, if AI reverses and real estate recovers we could enter an environment where the opposite occurs and real estate starts to operate like the countercyclical offset to an AI recession.

All that said, I think there are some very important differences between this environment and the 2002 downturn. That doesn’t mean there isn’t continued risk or that the broader stock market couldn’t fall further, but the probability of a broad 40%+ decline that lasts many years looks unlikely to me. So far this is looking more like a healthy correction than a recessionary downturn. And if it turns into a real recession I suspect lower interest rates are going to have a far greater impact than they did in years like 2002 or 2008. But again, if the AI recession is looming then those long duration tech stocks are still exposed to further adjustment.

What’s An Investor To Do?

It’s interesting to think about sequence of returns risk in the context of all this. This is a concept that is typically only applied to retirement. That is the risk of a large stock market downturn right when you retire so you get a poor sequence of returns that causes a debilitating withdrawal rate. While retirees are especially sensitive to this, sequence risk is actually the thing all investors are ALWAYS concerned with. The 25 year old who contributes 100K to an investment plan is also concerned about the sequence of their returns. They can typically afford for their stocks to fall 50% right after they invest, but it’s not something they want to live through. So good investing requires a plan that always mitigates sequence risk relative to your behavioral and financial planning needs. Total return strategies try to do this, but most of them are little more than taking long duration uncorrelated assets and trying to time when those long duration assets will operate like short duration assets. That doesn’t mean total return strategies are useless. It just means they’re more likely to look like long(er) duration assets because the manager can’t sustainably turn a long duration asset like stocks or gold into a short duration asset like t-bills or t-notes.

Of course, our solution is asset-liability matching because sequence risk mitigation is precisely what temporal matching does. And I think the current downturn is a significant validation of the overall Defined Duration framework. Anyone who has 0-5 years of liquidity built into their portfolio is unfazed by this downturn. If you’re loaded to the gills with long duration tech this is very uncomfortable because you have a potential asset-liability mismatch in your portfolio. But the 25 year old worker who has 80% in stocks and 20% set aside for that house down payment and emergency fund is unfazed by this because they don’t need the 80% of stocks in the next 5-10 years. The retiree who blocked out 0-7 years in shorter duration instruments is unfazed by this because they can ride out a very long stock bear market before they ever need to fund their portfolio from multi-asset instruments or stocks. There’s no reason for these people to become forced sellers of stocks. So on and so forth. Compartmentalizing your assets relative to your liabilities isn’t just a cute strategy run by pensions and banks. It’s a comprehensive investing process that works because it matches to a liability driven plan rather than constantly trying to optimize the assets in a world that is wholly unpredictable.

This is especially true in the context of total return strategies, which rely on asset optimization across different types of assets. The problem is, almost everything is falling simultaneously. Gold is down 35%, Bitcoin is down 40% and even managed futures are off 6%. So, even the things I refer to as “insurance” are down. The very best hedge this year hasn’t been gold, Bitcoin, long duration bonds or any alternative. It’s been short duration assets like Tbills and T-notes. If you didn’t have a temporal hedge in your portfolio in the last 12 months you’re most likely in a significant amount of total pain right now because every long duration is now either negative for the year or in the middle of a drawdown (long duration bonds have done slightly better of late, but are in a crushing long-term bear market and still negative on the year). This is what ALM is all about. It’s not about optimizing the assets and trying to time when a 30 year bond or other long duration asset will hedge your portfolio in the short-term. It’s about knowing that if you have any short-term need the ONLY instrument that can consistently immunize that liability (or behavioral need) is a well matched short duration asset.

I think our recent research piece “The Price of (Un)Certainty” is more important than when I published it a few weeks ago. Real rates are still 3%+ and investors who need certainty can still lock in certainty going out decades. But again, it all depends on your personal needs. The investor who needs certainty has better options today than they have in a long time because TIPS and shorter duration nominal bonds look so attractive. This also makes multi-asset instruments like 60/40 incrementally more attractive because the 40% piece can do real hedging now. And if equity valuations fall further you’ll start hearing me talk about how long duration assets just turned into short(er) duration assets that make them much more attractive for a statistical matching process. But that’s the thing about ALM – when time is your whole strategy you don’t have to worry about timing the market because your portfolio changes aren’t about turning water into wine (long duration assets into short duration assets). It’s about turning a dial when your plan changes and then considering which temporal asset is the appropriate match at that time.

Well, that’s all I’ve got for you this weekend. I hope everyone is hanging in there and as always, stay disciplined.

We had the one and only Meb Faber on for our first interview (you can watch here). I hope to turn the interviews into a real life version of my book, Your Perfect Portfolio, where we interview different types of investors and I probe them on how they build their own perfect portfolio. I hope we all learn a lot from it.

data.title: Do Term Spread Inversions Help Predict Australian Recessions?
data.description:
Do term spread inversions help predict Australian recessions? Not really, even using alternative recession chronologies.

Figure 1: Top panel,  Australia10 year-3 month term spread, %, and ECRI defined peak-to-trough recession dates shaded light blue, Middle panel, Light green denotes trough to peak unemployment rate defined dates. Melbourne Institute defined recession dates shaded light violet, Bottom panel, modified Sahm rule peak to trough (+0.75 ppt threshold). Unemployment rate available only starting 1978M02, so no Sahm rule based recession dates before 1979M02; end date is assumed equal to ECRI’s. Source: ECRI, Melbourne Institute, author’s calculations. 

While ECRI and the Melbourne Institute largely agree on the mid-1980’s and 1990-91 recessions, and agree on the no-2009 recession call, they do disagree on the 1970’s recessions.

Interestingly, the Sahm rule (with a 75 bps threshold instead of 50 bps, as suggested by the RBA), would posit a recession in 2001 and 2009. However, total employment as well as GDP do not decline on a sustained basis.

None of these recession are predicted with an pseudo-R2 greater than 0.14 over 1986-26m (the coefficient on the spread is opposite of expected). Restricting the sample to the pre-pandemic period raises the pseudo-R2 to up to 50% for ECRI or Melbourne Institute chronologies; but the spread still retains the “wrong” sign.

Note that the lack of predictive power for recessions is different from lack of predictive power for, say, GDP growth (e.g., Poke, Wells, 2009).

data.title: Will There Be Another Government Shutdown This Year?
data.description:
I’d like to see a shutdown or continuing resolution for the rest of the year. But what are the odds?

The above Government Shutdown graph is from Polymarket, with my highlights and arrows.

At times there is little difference between December 12 and December 31. Other times, like now there is a substantial difference between the two dates.

Currently the odds for December 12 are 24 percent. The odds for December 31 are 36 percent.

Key Dates

  • December 11: The current continuing resolution (H.R. 6500 / Public Law 119-103) funds federal agencies through 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on Friday, December 11, 2026. After that moment, the money runs out unless Congress passes (and the President signs) new funding before then.

  • December 17: The last scheduled House session day is December 17, 2026.

  • December 18: The last scheduled Senate session day is December 18, 2026.

  • December 19: Congress leaves for the Christmas/holiday recess. The 119th Congress’s term officially ends. Hooray!!

  • January 3, 2027: 120th Congress convenes at noon on January 3, 2027

The Dec 17-19 are published targets. They can shift if unfinished business (especially the December 11 funding deadline) keeps them in session longer, but the plan is to finish before Christmas and not return until the new Congress begins.

Continuing Resolution

There is no Polymarket contract on another continuing resolution, but this is what would happen.

If Congress passes (and the President signs) another continuing resolution that funds the government through December 31, 2026 (or into early January 2027):

  • There would be no funding lapse on December 12 or later in December. Agencies would keep operating at roughly the current levels.

  • The next deadline would fall after the current (119th) Congress ends. The new 120th Congress — with Democratic majorities in both chambers — takes office at noon on January 3, 2027. Any further funding bill would then be negotiated and passed under the new majority.

  • Pending legislation that doesn’t pass before adjournment generally dies and has to start over.

A short extension past the 11th remains possible, but it doesn’t guarantee funding stays in place through year-end without further action. That is the main reason the “December 31” odds are higher than the “by December 12” odds.

In short, a year-end CR is the classic “kick the can” move. It clears the immediate December cliff but leaves the real spending decisions for the incoming Congress.

Republicans do not want to kick the can here. Yet, they do not have the votes to get what Trump wants.

Why I Support a Shutdown

I would like to see all funding, especially for the war and ICE to be frozen in place until the next Congress. A continuing resolution with no additional funding would also suffice.

Then I want to see funding for ICE totally removed and military spending reduced.

Unfortunately, there is roughly no chance of ICE funding removed and military spending reduced, but the less funding all around for anything, the happier I am.

On the plus side, I do not believe Trump and Hegseth will get all the military funding they seek. Expect Senate compromises for which Thune will get the blame.

Importantly, the harder Hegseth and Trump push for full military funding without offsetting budget cuts, the less likely they get anything.

So let the Republican bickering and infighting continue. The more the better because we are heading into the lamest of lame duck final two years.

data.title: Kroger Lays Off American Workers, Moves Jobs To India
data.description:
Kroger (KR) has started laying off about 3,000 American white-collar workers at the same time it’s developing an operations center in India that is hiring dozens of workers.

That puts the company, which has described itself as “America’s favorite grocer,” at odds with how most Americans feel about U.S. jobs being outsourced overseas.  

“Overall, when Americans are asked what hurts American workers, the top answers are outsourcing jobs to other countries (80% of Americans think this hurts U.S. jobholders), more foreign-made products being sold in the U.S. (77% think this hurts), increased use of contract or temporary employees (57%), automation of jobs (50%) and the decline in union membership (49%),” a 2016 Pew Research poll showed.

Kroger has already started notifying workers at its Cincinnati headquarters. It will also be making cuts in other cities where it maintains corporate offices, according to the Cincinnati Business Courier.

And while the cuts have already begun, the company has not shared a timetable for when the full 3,000 would be let go.

The company has, however, moved forward with its plans to launch an operations center in Bangalore, India, and has begun hiring workers there.

A request to Kroger Investor Relations to comment on this story was not immediately returned.

Kroger makes a risky move

While sending jobs to India will help Kroger CEO Gregory Foran’s plan to slash $5 billion in costs from the company that it plans to invest in lower prices, it’s a move that risks alienating customers.

A research paper co-authored by Wharton marketing professor Stefano Puntoni “finds that consumers react far more negatively when layoffs are caused by offshoring. In other words, sending jobs abroad does not just affect the workers — it dents the company’s image, too.”

The paper’s key point is based around what the researchers call the “social contract” — the unspoken expectation that firms should support the communities they operate in.

“When a company cuts domestic jobs and moves them overseas, consumers often view it as a betrayal of that norm — even if the move makes business sense on paper,” Knowledge at Wharton shared.

That’s something Puntoni talked about in an interview with Wharton Business Daily.

“We found significantly more negative conversations about collective layoffs when they were about offshoring than about automation,” he said.

Kroger begins outsourcing jobs

Foran has talked about the new facility, but he didn’t actually mention where it was during his comments in Kroger’s fourth-quarter earnings call.

“To support our modernization efforts, we are launching the Kroger Global Capability Center. This initiative is designed to streamline decision-making, improve productivity, and increase the speed at which we execute on behalf of our customers,” he said.

The Kroger CEO focused on the work that would be done at the facility without mentioning that it would be located offshore.

“It complements the work already underway across the organization to modernize how we operate. Work has started and is progressing with speed. We expect modest benefits in 2026 with more significant benefits expected in 2027 and 2028,” he added.

What is the Kroger Capability Center hiring for?

The website talent500.com shows nearly 30 job titles, all in Bangalore, the capital of India’s southern state of Karnataka. LinkedIn also has similar listings, the Cincinnati Business Courier first reported.

The positions include senior real estate portfolio specialist, senior audit analyst, supply chain analyst, lead financial analyst, and logistics operations specialist.

One job listing is looking for a “Manager, Supply Chain Analytics” and requires 7-11 years of experience. The description makes it clear that it’s a high-level position.

“Lead advanced supply chain analytics and modeling that support network strategy, flow strategy, capacity planning, and strategic decision-making. Own the repeatable data foundation, models, dashboards, and scenario analysis needed to evaluate cost, service, capacity, inventory, and operational trade-offs,” the site shared.

Kroger does not list a salary range, but Payscale shows similar jobs in the region averaging 2.8 million rupees, or about $29,500 a year.

In Cincinnati, Payscale shows that an experienced supply chain manager’s median base is $99k, with the 90th percentile at $131,000.

Kroger walks a risky road

While it’s fairly common for large American technology companies to offshore some of their employees, it feels a little different when it’s being done by a grocery chain serving local U.S. neighborhoods.

Microsoft (MSFT) and Apple (AAPL), for example, have a global product, and it makes sense for them to operate in offices around the world.

Kroger, however, only operates in the U.S. The chain has 2,697 stores in 35 states and the District of Columbia.

But it’s also worth noting that Kroger has little choice when it comes to making cuts, according to retail expert Brittain Ladd.

“The layoffs are happening because Kroger’s cost structure has been under pressure for years. The company deferred decisions on outsourcing and technology that many of its competitors made a decade ago, and those decisions are now being made under CEO Greg Foran,” he posted on his LinkedIn page.

Ladd did not comment on the offshoring, but made it clear the company needed to lower its costs.

“As a former consultant to Kroger, I believe the company has little choice but to transform. Maintaining the status quo is not an option,” he wrote.

data.title: Have Investors Learned The Lesson Of The Year 2000 DotComTech Wreck?

Last Friday, the technology-heavy Nasdaq lost over 5% wiping out all of its 2026 gains. Nasdaq has entered “correction territory” with many analysts forecasting additional losses to come.

Nvidia (NVDA), once the darling of Wall Street, lost over 50% of its multi-trillion valuation resulting from the Jensen Huang scandal. Facing an SEC investigation of its accounting for “circular financing” of chip sales, one wonders if this is a redux of the 2001 Enron debacle which exposed the labyrinth of the “raptors” off-book partnerships which brought down the energy trading firm and led to criminal convictions of its top executives.

The Anthropic (ANT) blockbuster IPO added $80 billion of AI technology equity to the market and saw its stock price fall below its IPO  level with investors questioning if the company’s revenue and profit forecasts are illusory.

The current market concern is reminiscent of the year 2000 popping of the “Dot Com” bubble when high flying technology stocks crashed, leaving retail investors holding an empty bag. Some of the stock “names” suffering huge losses today are  the same names that led the wipeout in 2000—Intel (INTC), Oracle (ORCL), Cisco, Qualcomm (QCOM), Micron (MU) and Nvidia which had drawdowns of 50 to 60%.

Retail investors and their Financial Advisors burned in 2000 should have learned a lesson to diversify and not overconcentrate their portfolios in tech names. They also should have learned that margin borrowing could lead to outsized losses when stock prices fall.

Unfortunately, many investors and their advisors forgot the lessons of the Dot Com crash and are getting burned once again.

New York, New York, November 18th, 2026, Chainwire


Powered by Noah's regulated payments infrastructure, Tria's new Currency Accounts let eligible users send euros from their bank and receive USDC in their self-custodial Tria Wallet, usually within minutes, without a crypto exchange or card-based on-ramp.

Tria, the self-custodial neofinance platform, today announced the rollout of Currency Accounts, a new funding capability powered by regulated payments infrastructure provider Noah that connects traditional bank transfers directly to self-custodial wallets through automatic EUR-to-USDC conversion.

After completing a one-time identity check, eligible users receive personal EUR account details, including an IBAN, inside the Tria app. They can then send euros through a standard SEPA bank transfer and receive USDC directly in their self-custodial wallet, usually within minutes. SWIFT transfers are also supported.

The process eliminates the need to first deposit funds on a centralized crypto exchange, purchase digital assets with a card or complete a separate conversion. Noah handles the underlying banking, foreign exchange and compliance infrastructure, while Tria provides the self-custodial wallet where users receive and manage their funds. Tria does not hold users' euros as a bank balance; incoming funds are automatically converted to USDC and delivered to their wallets.

"People shouldn't need an exchange account or a series of transactions just to move money from their bank into a wallet they control," said Vijit Katta, CEO and co-founder of Tria. "We're making that process as familiar as a standard bank transfer. You send euros from your bank, and USDC arrives in Tria, ready to use. That's a significant improvement in how people access onchain finance."
"Moving money into a stablecoin wallet should be as simple as sending a message,” said Shah Ramezani, founder and CEO at Noah. “Noah makes the banking, FX and compliance invisible, so a Tria user simply sends euros and USDC arrives. That's what regulated payments infrastructure should do: take complexity away from the user and simplify stablecoin on ramps.”

The launch gives European users a direct route from their existing bank accounts into Tria's financial ecosystem, including its spending and trading capabilities. It also simplifies access for freelancers, people receiving euro-denominated payments and users who want to move money onchain without relying on a centralized exchange. A Tria Card is not required.

EUR is Tria's first supported fiat currency, with additional currencies planned. The new capability currently supports incoming transfers only; EUR withdrawals to bank accounts are not available through this feature.

Access is rolling out gradually and is expected to reach the full eligible user base over approximately two weeks.

About Tria

Tria is a self-custodial neofinance platform bringing spending, trading and digital asset management into a unified financial experience. data.title: Mysteries Of The AI Bubble: Where’s The Consumption?
data.description:
Many of us who have been warning of an AI bubble have raised the prospect of a big hit to consumption if the bubble bursts. We base this concern on the conventional view that there is a stock wealth effect on consumption of roughly 3 cents on a dollar. 

This means that if the market were to lose 30 percent of its value (it lost 50 percent in the collapse of the tech bubble), it would eliminate roughly $24 trillion in stock wealth. With a wealth effect of 3 percent, this would translate into a hit to annual consumption of $720 billion, a bit more than 2 percent of GDP. A hit of this magnitude, coupled with the collapse of the AI investment boom, would almost certainly be large enough to throw the economy into a recession.  

Jason Furman has challenged this view, arguing that it seems that the wealth effect on consumption has been much smaller in the years since the pandemic, just 1 cent on the dollar. He points to the fact that the consumption share of GDP does not seem to be especially high at present, meaning that it doesn’t look like the huge increase in stock wealth in the last five years has had much impact on consumption.

This leaves us with a story where we either believe something has changed in the longstanding relationship between stock wealth and consumption or alternatively, that we are missing something. I’m going to explore the “we are missing something” route.

Specifically, I am not sure that people always see savings and consumption the way economists measure them. In this case, the issue would be how they treat the money they spend on buying a home and related expenses like property tax and insurance. In the GDP accounts, the purchase of a home is treated as investment, a form of savings. Similarly, the monthly mortgage payment, as well as property taxes and insurance, are not counted directly at all. They are supposed to be picked up through owners’ equivalent rent, since these expenses should be among the costs driving up rent.

The definitional issues don’t really matter in terms of accounting for consumption and saving, as long as housing costs track rents more or less closely, as has generally been the case. However, this has not been true since the pandemic. (It also wasn’t the case in the housing bubble.)

As can be seen, adjusted for overall inflation, the cost of buying a house has outpaced the cost of renting by around 20 percent since the pandemic. This means, other things equal, homeowners would be paying about 20 percent more on their monthly mortgage payments, taxes, and insurance than if house prices had just risen in step with rents.1 

Suppose that people acted as though this additional 20 percent they are paying on their mortgage and other related ownership costs were consumption and not investment. In the third quarter of this year, the imputed value of owners’ equivalent rent (OER) was $2,652 billion. If this were increased by 20 percent, in line with the gap between house prices and rent, that would increase spending on OER by $530 billion, or 1.6 percent of GDP. It would imply a corresponding reduction in savings. This adjustment would get us considerably closer to the 3 percent estimate of the wealth effect on consumption.

The relevant issue for a collapse of an AI-driven stock bubble is how a plunge in stock wealth would affect this picture. My speculation is that if we continue to see the stock prices of the big AI companies plunge, eager buyers for expensive houses would vanish, and some current owners look to sell to make up for their reduced stock portfolios. That should lower house prices, a good story in my book. Also, we may see some house owners look to cut spending in other areas if they don’t see their housing wealth as part of their targeted savings. (If house prices fall, then there would be a negative wealth effect on consumption from this as well.)

This story is clearly speculative, and I’m generally inclined to say that we should accept the accounting categories that God gave us. But when we have a seeming anomaly, like a sudden shrinking of the size of the stock wealth effect, it is worth trying to beat up our categories a bit to see if we might be missing something.

  1. Homeowners’ insurance, which is not included in the CPI, has hugely outpaced the overall inflation rate over the last decade, presumably due in large part to the effects of global warming. The larger amount that people are now spending on homeowners’ insurance would not directly affect consumption and savings. It would only be picked up indirectly through its effect on owners equivalent rent.

data.title: Hashi Mainnet is Live With 20-Plus Partners, Bringing Bitcoin Finance to Sui at Scale
data.description:
Grand Cayman, Cayman Islands, November 19th, 2026, Chainwire


Anchorage Digital, Fluid, HoneyB, and Upshift support institutional and retail access to Bitcoin on Sui with BitGo, Inc. expected to follow in 2027

Hashi, Sui's native Bitcoin finance infrastructure, is now live on mainnet, with more than 20 custody, retail, and DeFi participants.

Bitcoin has spent years becoming one of the world's largest pools of capital. Now the infrastructure to put it to work has arrived, forming one of the broadest coalitions in Bitcoin finance. 

That coalition is still growing fast. The latest to join Hashi are Merkl, an onchain incentive platform; and Current, a lending protocol. These additions expand the ecosystem of DeFi products and services being built around Bitcoin on Sui.

Bitcoin-Native Finance, Now Live

Hashi keeps Bitcoin on the Bitcoin network and mints hBTC, a 1:1 Bitcoin-backed asset, on Sui. That hBTC can then serve as collateral for lending, borrowing, and other onchain financial products. 

Hashi is decentralized by design. It's secured by validators, not a single entity, using industry-leading cryptography. On top of that foundation, it connects leading providers across custody, trading, and decentralized finance to build financial products, giving Bitcoin holders many ways to put their assets to work.

Accessing Bitcoin Finance on Sui

With hBTC now live, Bitcoin holders have a new set of opportunities at their fingertips. That starts with borrowing against BTC and accessing new financial strategies through lending markets and vaults. 

To meet the specific needs of institutions, several new providers are offering new lending and vault facilities. 

Fluid’s institutional-grade lending protocol is now live on Sui, beginning with Bitcoin-backed stablecoin loans. Bitcoin holders can use Hashi to bring BTC onto Sui as hBTC, then use it as collateral on Fluid to borrow stablecoins, starting with USDC with more flows coming. 

“Bitcoin is the largest pool of idle capital in crypto,” said Samyak Jain, founder and CEO at Fluid. “With Hashi, it can now power deep, capital-efficient credit markets on Fluid.”

Institutional Access, Retail Opportunities, and Liquidity

For institutions, that infrastructure shows up as a custody problem solved. Institutions will be able to use both leading crypto custodians, Anchorage Digital and BitGo, Inc. (“BitGo”) to access Hashi. This model gives institutions a path to hold or deploy BTC into Hashi. Previously announced institutional partners, such as Cumberland and Wave Digital Assets will all play roles as early participants in deploying BTC and stablecoins on Hashi, providing liquidity to a variety of strategies on Sui. Sui DeFi protocols, including Blueprint Finance (Concrete), Bluefin, Cetus, Current, and Suilend will also unlock new lending opportunities, stablecoin credit, and yield strategies backed by Bitcoin. 

“Some of the world's largest Bitcoin holders are sitting on enormous amounts of untapped financial potential,” said Nathan McCauley, CEO and Co-Founder at Anchorage Digital. “Hashi gives our institutional clients a new way to access Bitcoin finance on Sui, with their BTC held in custody at Anchorage Digital Bank.”

If you’re an institution interested in deploying BTC or stablecoins on Hashi, please reach out to your custodian or [email protected]. Users can explore more at sui.io/hashi. 

About Sui

Sui, where money moves as freely as messages, is a next-generation Layer 1 blockchain built for agentic finance and scalable global payments. Founded by the core team behind Meta’s stablecoin initiative and powered by an object-centric model, Sui makes assets, permissions, and user data programmable and ownable. Sui’s primitives offer builders everything they need to create high-performance payments and financial applications, including instant agentic payments. Learn more at sui.io.

data.title: Inflation Expectations Plummet. The Fed Is On Track To Make Another Policy Mistake.
data.description:
The Federal Reserve raised rates during an external oil shock. Now commodities, gasoline, and inflation expectations are falling rapidly, and the forward curve remains in deep backwardation, signaling disinflation. However, the cost of tight money will linger long after the spike is gone.

The FOMC minutes of the October meeting show that almost all participants judged that further hikes would likely be appropriate. In fact, two members dissented in favor of an immediate increase, and Governor Christopher Waller mentioned a half-point move in December to “shock people.” He defended a rate cut in January despite elevated core PCE and rising inflation expectations, while also discussing a large rate hike as those figures rapidly reversed. However, the market has already moved on.

Commodities are falling fast, inflation expectations are plummeting, and the first alternative-data estimates for November point to a negative monthly CPI print. Once again, central banks are fighting yesterday’s war with a tool that does nothing to change its cause.

The cause was never excess demand or an overheated economy. Money velocity remains contained at 1.47, money supply growth comes mostly from government spending, and there are no signs of excess credit-taking or unsustainable demand growth. Rather, the opposite. The 2026 CPI surge came from the war with Iran and the disruption of flows through the Strait of Hormuz, a supply shock imported from the Persian Gulf, with no relation to an overheated American consumer or a spend-price spiral.

In the past month, the shock has been reversing, and fast. Brent has lost about a fifth of its value in November as Middle East supplies recovered to pre-war levels. Over the past month, gasoline futures have dropped almost 20% and heating oil nearly 21%. Copper is down 16%, silver 28%, wheat 11% and sugar 17%, while the CRB index has dropped more than 10% and the S&P GSCI almost 13%. Furthermore, the average retail price of gasoline has fallen to roughly $3.65 a gallon, down about 15% in a month and close to the $3.50 threshold that consumers consider more concerning.

The impact on prices is immediate. The Bloomberg Price Index points to a 0.1% monthly decline in November. Energy subtracts more than a quarter of a percentage point, while core goods are basically flat. If confirmed, it would be the first negative monthly print since June. Headline annual inflation still looks high, at 4.2%. However, that number is the rear-view mirror of the oil spike, and it will fall rapidly as base effects and lower energy prices feed through.

Market participants understand this. One-year USD inflation swaps have collapsed from above 3.5% in the spring to below 2%, and two-year swaps are near 2.1%. More importantly, long-term expectations never de-anchored. The 30-year inflation swap barely moved through the entire Iran geopolitical risk episode, staying within the 2.3%-2.5% band. The single most important variable for the Fed, inflation expectations, showed that investors viewed the shock as temporary. Core PCE expectations also proved more stable than hawkish Fed members suggested.

Core PCE inflation remained at 3.0% year on year in June, July, and August and barely rose to 3.1% in September, far from the ludicrous concept of a “second-round” inflation burst that hawkish Fed members warned about. Forecasts were clear as well. The Philadelphia Fed’s survey left its core PCE projections unchanged at 3.3% for 2026 and 2.4% for 2027, while cutting its ten-year PCE inflation expectation to 2.20%. The Fed’s own September projections kept core PCE for 2027 at 2.5%, exactly as in the June estimate, with 2026 revised up by just one tenth of a point. However, the same committee increased its expected federal funds rate for 2027 from 3.6% to 4.1%. Half a point of additional tightening for an unchanged medium-term inflation outlook shows a policy driven by fear of headlines.

It is incredible to see that central bank rhetoric is the most hawkish in years. J.P. Morgan’s NLP Hawk-Dove score for the Fed has climbed above 30, close to the levels of 2022. Monetary authorities are synchronizing their tightening measures at the same time that the commodity impulse is fading.

Hawks will argue that core CPI rose 0.3% for three consecutive months and that energy has passed through to core goods and services. However, that pass-through was almost nonexistent, and the individual transport and goods prices that did rise because diesel soared are falling now. Fed officials seem to ignore that prices are determined by demand, not costs.

Monetary policy works with lags of twelve to eighteen months. Hiking today to fight a nonexistent second-round effect means the full burden of tighter policy appears when the shock has disappeared, accelerating a Fed-engineered private sector contraction instead of preventing inflation.

Inflation is always a monetary phenomenon. When the price of oil soars without an excess of money creation, families and businesses spend more on energy and less on everything else. That is a change in relative prices, and it reverses when the supply disruption ends. Raising rates to combat it is like treating a broken leg with chemotherapy. The patient suffers the terrible side effects, and the leg heals on its own anyway.

Rate hikes have made credit more expensive for families and small businesses at the worst time and done nothing to reduce government spending. In fact, rate hikes have inflated the interest expense of a heavily indebted federal government. Even Citigroup warns that US interest rates are “unsustainably high,” with falling equity valuations and risks to AI investment threatening growth, and that easing energy prices and tighter financial conditions could eventually push the Fed into an urgent 180-degree move to a dovish stance as the economy weakens and financial risks rise. Citi still expects an interest rate hike in December, followed by a hold, and then cuts later in 2027. That is the classic central bank pattern of hiking into the peak and cutting into the slump.

The Federal Reserve claims to be data dependent. It does not show it. The data are clear. Oil is down a fifth in a month, gasoline is heading below $3.50, commodity indices are in freefall, alternative-data nowcasts point to negative monthly inflation, and market-based expectations are back below the 2% target in the short term and stable in the long term.

Hiking in December would be stubbornness disguised as credibility.

The Fed engineered a market sell-off and decided to hurt families and businesses with a series of misguided rate hikes when there was no sign of an overheated economy, just an external energy shock. Now that the damage has been done, it is stubbornly talking about rate hikes.

There is nothing in the job market or core inflation pointing to the need for rate hikes.

Commodity disinflation lowers the Taylor-rule interest-rate estimate, while money supply and velocity do not justify further tightening. The trend in commodities and CPI estimates, which are negative for November, shows that, under the lower-neutral-rate limit, the implied Fed funds rate should be below current levels, even supporting a rate cut.

Central banks failed to see the 2021 inflation coming because they ignored the monetary excess they created. In 2026, they are making the opposite mistake, treating an external supply shock affecting individual prices as if it were a monetary problem impacting aggregate prices. The result will be the same. Another policy mistake.

Demolishing the private sector and engineering a market crash with unwarranted rate hikes is not a sign of independence but evidence of irresponsibility.
